Reward Learning from Best-of-NN Preference Data:
Targets, Tradeoffs, and Design Principles

Rattana Pukdee rpukdee@cs.cmu.edu Affiliation: Machine Learning Department Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Maria-Florina Balcan ninamf@cs.cmu.edu Affiliation: Machine Learning Department Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Pradeep Ravikumar pkr@cs.cmu.edu Affiliation: Machine Learning Department Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Best-of-NN sampling is widely used to construct pairwise preference data: NN candidates are drawn from a base distribution, and the best is paired with a rejected response. Despite its widespread use, what Bradley–Terry (BT) reward learning extracts from such data, and how to choose NN and the base distribution, remain unclear. We specialize a recent analysis of preference data via its induced conditional distribution to Best-of-NN. For independent-reference variants, we derive closed-form reward targets as explicit functions of NN and the base distribution, and show that they preserve the latent reward ranking. For the practical Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst variants, chosen and rejected responses are coupled through the same candidate set, so exact BT representability generally fails; nevertheless, bounded-class minimizers approach the reference targets as NN grows. Although margin and connectivity are known to govern sample efficiency in pairwise preference learning, Best-of-NN couples them through NN in opposing directions: larger NN widens pairwise margins but reduces connectivity. This trade-off yields two design principles: use larger NN when preference labels are the bottleneck, smaller NN when generation is the bottleneck; and shape the base distribution to place mass between the responses whose comparison matters most at test time. Experiments on synthetic and real preference data support the predicted dependence on sample size and base-distribution shape. 11 1 Code available at: https://github.com/rattaoup/bon-preference

1 Introduction

Pairwise preference data is a general and increasingly important supervision signal in machine learning. It has been extensively studied in the literature on learning to rank (Cao et al., 2007; Wauthier et al., 2013) and learning preference (Fürnkranz and Hüllermeier, 2010; Qian et al., 2015), learning combinatorial functions (Balcan et al., 2016) and more recently has become central to modern AI systems, especially in reward learning and post-training of large language models (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022). This form of supervision is widely used because relative judgements are often easier to obtain, from both human annotators and increasingly AI evaluators (Zheng et al., 2023), than calibrated scalar scores.

In modern AI systems, pairwise preference data is often used to train reward models, typically with a Bradley-Terry objective, and these reward models may then be used to further optimize a language model through reinforcement learning (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). Preference data is also used more directly in fine-tuning the model as well (Rafailov et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2024). A common approach to construct the preference data is through Best-of-NN sampling. For a given context, NN responses are sampled from a base distribution, and an oracle identifies the best response as the chosen one. The rejected response is then selected either uniformly from the remaining N−1N-1 responses (Best-vs-Random) or as the worst response (Best-vs-Worst). The special case N=2N=2 recovers the standard pairwise-comparison setting (Christiano et al., 2017). The common intuition is that larger NN improves this data, since the chosen response is better in absolute terms. We show this intuition is incomplete: what matters is not only the quality of the chosen response, but which comparisons the dataset makes available. We study reward learning as a clean lens on the role of data with two fundamental questions.

  1. 1.

    When preference data is generated through Best-of-N sampling, what reward function is induced by the resulting dataset under Bradley-Terry objective?

  2. 2.

    How should the candidate-set size N and the base distribution be chosen ?

Our analysis builds on a recent distribution-agnostic framework (Pukdee et al., 2026) that analyzes preference data through the conditional preference distribution (CPRD), characterizing when it is Bradley-Terry representable and showing that finite-sample learning is governed by margin and comparison connectivity. That framework leaves the induced reward targets, margins, and connectivity abstract, since they depend on the data-generation mechanism. We instantiate it for Best-of-NN preference data, where the order-statistic structure makes these quantities concrete and reveals how they scale with NN. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    Targets: We study a clean reference setting in which the rejected response is sampled independently. In this setting, we characterize the reward targets induced by Best-of-NN preference data in closed form and show that they preserve the ranking of an underlying ground-truth reward. This identifies what signal reward learning is recovering from the data. For the practical Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst settings, we show that the corresponding population minimizers do not admit the same clean characterization, but approach these reference targets as NN grows.

  2. 2.

    Tradeoffs: We show that NN controls a fundamental tradeoff between margin and comparison connectivity. Increasing NN pushes chosen responses toward the top of the reward distribution, which amplifies pairwise margins and makes individual comparisons more informative. But this same concentration narrows the range of responses being compared, reducing comparison connectivity and leaving intermediate comparisons underrepresented. These two effects pull in opposite directions and govern sample efficiency.

  3. 3.

    Design principles: We derive two actionable guidelines. The candidate-set size NN should be chosen based on the resource bottleneck: larger NN is more helpful when preference labels are scarce, whereas smaller NN is often preferable when preference labels are cheap and data is abundant. Beyond choosing NN, the base distribution itself is also a design lever through what we call the between-mass principle: the induced margin between two responses grows with the amount of base-distribution mass placed between them in reward order. Shaping the base distribution to put mass between the response pairs that matter under the target evaluation distribution selectively amplifies those margins. We validate these predictions on both synthetic and real preference data.

Taken together, our results provide a learning-theoretic foundation for reward learning from Best-of-NN preference data, while yielding concrete principles for data design in practice.

2 Related work

Best-of-NN Sampling for Inference and Training. Best-of-NN sampling (BoN) is an inference-time method with strong empirical performance (Stiennon et al., 2020; Cobbe et al., 2021b; Nakano et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2024). The idea is to sample NN responses from a policy and select the one with the highest reward. Despite its simplicity, BoN is a strong baseline for inference-time scaling (Snell et al., 2024). Various works have studied the theoretical properties of the induced BoN policy (Huang et al., 2025b), including its distance from the reference policy and its win rate (Beirami et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024a), and the soft BoN variants (Verdun et al., 2025; Aminian et al., 2025). These results suggest that win rate increases with NN. However, larger NN does not always improve performance in practice; when NN is too large, reward hacking can degrade output quality (Gao et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025a). Given the effectiveness of BoN but its NN-fold inference cost, several works aim to train a policy that matches the BoN distribution while requiring only a single sample at inference time. This can be done offline with a fixed BoN dataset (Touvron et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2023; Amini et al., 2025) or iteratively (Sessa et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024). Gui et al. (2024) provide theoretical analysis for this training time setting, showing that the BoN distribution is optimal in terms of win rate against the base model for a given KL distance budget. While this literature clarifies the role of BoN in improving generation quality and policy training, it leaves open the question of how BoN affects learning when it is used to construct preference data.

Learning from Best-of-NN Preference Data. Understanding how preference data affects the final model is an important question, since it can inform the design of better datasets. Recent work suggests that better preference data leads to better downstream policies (Ivison et al., 2024; Morimura et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025). In this literature, however, better preference data is often identified using external proxies such as reward-model scores. While a higher score may indicate that a response is better in an absolute sense, it does not necessarily mean that the resulting pairwise comparison is more informative for preference learning. We study a related question from a different perspective: rather than analyzing the end-to-end policy outcome, we stop at the reward-learning stage and ask how the preference data shapes the learned reward function. This provides a cleaner view of the effect of the data itself, without conflating it with the base policy’s behavior. Razin et al. () study the complementary direction, linking reward properties to downstream policy performance, closing the loop from data to policy.

In practice, preference data can be constructed in several ways, including by comparing responses from language models of different capacities (Kim et al., 2023), using different prompts to produce chosen and rejected responses (Yang et al., 2024b), or, most commonly, by sampling multiple responses from the same base model and using a human annotator, reward model, or model-based judge to identify preferred and dispreferred responses from the candidate set (Bai et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024). In this paper, we focus on the last setting, namely Best-of-NN preference data. Prior work has studied this setting empirically for reward learning: Pace et al. (2024) show that selecting the best and worst candidates from a pool can improve reward-model training, while Yuan et al. (2024) study settings in which the language model itself is also used to provide reward feedback. We ask a more foundational question: what reward function is induced when pairwise comparisons are generated through Best-of-NN sampling?

3 Problem Setup

In practice, Best-of-NN (BoN) preference data pipelines may rely on human annotators, reward models, or LLM judges to identify preferred responses. We study a clean theoretical abstraction of this setting in which preferences are induced by an underlying latent reward function r∗r^{*}, even though r∗r^{*} itself is never observed. This abstraction allows us to ask what reward function is learned from the resulting comparison data.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a context space and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be a set of outcomes. Assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} are finite but can be exponentially large. Let r∗:𝒳×𝒴→ℝr^{*}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} be a target latent reward function. The supervision signal is in the form of pairwise comparison data where triplets (x,y+,y−)(x,y^{+},y^{-}) indicate that a chosen outcome y+y^{+} is preferred over a rejected outcome y−y^{-} given a context xx i.e. the latent reward r∗​(x,y+)>r∗​(x,y−)r^{*}(x,y^{+})>r^{*}(x,y^{-}).

To construct the pairwise preference data, the chosen outcome y+y^{+} is sampled from the Best-of-NN mechanism. First, we sample NN outcomes from a base distribution y1,…,yN∼Pbase(⋅∣x)y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\sim P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x), the outcome with the highest reward score is the chosen outcome, y+=arg⁡maxyi​r∗​(x,yi)y^{+}=\arg\max_{y_{i}}r^{*}(x,y_{i}). This procedure only requires access to an oracle that can identify the best outcome among NN candidates, rather than access to the reward scores r∗​(x,yi)r^{*}(x,y_{i}) themselves. This is a common approach in practice to construct pairwise preference data. For the rejected outcome y−y^{-}, two dominant approaches are

  • •

    Best-vs-Random (Khaki et al., 2024; Ivison et al., 2024): we sample y−y^{-} from {y1,…,yN}∖{y+}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\}\setminus\{y^{+}\} uniformly at random.

  • •

    Best-vs-Worst (Pace et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024): the outcome with the lowest reward score among {y1,…,yN}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\} is the rejected outcome, y−=arg⁡minyi​r∗​(x,yi)y^{-}=\arg\min_{y_{i}}r^{*}(x,y_{i}). This may require another oracle call to identify the worst outcome.

Whenever we observe a collision y+=y−y^{+}=y^{-}, we discard the triplet. Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst guarantee that the latent reward score y+y^{+} is always higher than y−y^{-}. Let PP be the probability distribution of the BoN preference data. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a hypothesis class of reward functions. A common learning objective for reward learning is Bradley-Terry (BT) objective given by

ℒP​(r)=𝔼P​[−log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,y+)−r⁡(x,y−))]\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[-\log\sigma(r(x,y^{+})-r(x,y^{-}))\right] (1)

when σ⁡(t)=11+e−t\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}} is the sigmoid function. Since the loss only depends on the difference between the reward scores of the chosen and rejected outcomes, r⁡(x,y+)−r⁡(x,y−)r(x,y^{+})-r(x,y^{-}), the reward is identifiable only up to an additive constant. To fix this ambiguity, we restrict ℋ\mathcal{H} to normalized reward functions satisfying 𝔼(x,y)∼μ​[r⁡(x,y)]=0\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mu}[r(x,y)]=0 for a fixed reference distribution μ\mu over 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. For example, this can be a uniform distribution. Finally, we define some notations that will be useful for our analysis. First, score quantiles F⁡(x,y)F(x,y) capture the probability that a random outcome from the base distribution Pbase(⋅∣x)P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x) has a lower or strictly lower reward score than the reward of yy.

3.1Strict and Inclusive Score Quantiles.

For any outcome y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, define the strict quantile

F−(x,y):=Pry′∼Pbase(⋅∣x)[r∗(x,y′)<r∗(x,y)]F^{-}(x,y):=\Pr_{y^{\prime}\sim P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x)}[\,r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})<r^{*}(x,y)\,] (2)

as the probability that a randomly drawn outcome from the base distribution has strictly lower reward than yy. We also define the inclusive quantile

F(x,y):=Pry′∼Pbase(⋅∣x)[r∗(x,y′)≤r∗(x,y)]=F−(x,y)+Pbase(y∣x).F(x,y):=\Pr_{y^{\prime}\sim P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x)}[\,r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})\leq r^{*}(x,y)\,]=F^{-}(x,y)+P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x). (3)

We also define pairwise margin,

3.2Margin.

For any reward function rr and any context xx and outcomes y,y′y,y^{\prime}, the pairwise margin of rr is given by

Δr​(x,y,y′):=r⁡(x,y)−r⁡(x,y′)\Delta_{r}(x;y,y^{\prime}):=r(x,y)-r(x,y^{\prime}) (4)

With these definitions in hand, we turn to our first question: what reward function does BoN preference data induce?

4 Characterizing the Learned Reward

We begin with the infinite data setting and analyze the minimizer of the population risk (equation 1). For analysis, we first define reference variants Best-vs-Independent and Best-vs-Worst-Independent, where the negative sample is drawn independently from the base distribution and the Worst-of-N sampling respectively. These variants have a much cleaner analysis and we will later on connect it back to the practical settings of Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst. We will use subscript B​R,B​W,B​I,B​W​IBR,BW,BI,BWI to denote if the data distribution and the reward function corresponds to Best-vs-Random, Best-vs-Worst, Best-vs-Independent and Best-vs-Worst-Independent respectively.

4.1 Independent Rejected Outcome

We start with the Best-vs-Independent scenario. The rejected outcome is independent of the chosen one, we can factorize the probability mass of PBIP_{\text{BI}} as

PBI​(x,y+,y−)=P⁡(x)​PBoN​(y+∣x)​Pbase​(y−∣x)P_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{+},y^{-})=P(x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{+}\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{-}\mid x) (5)

where PBoN​(y∣x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x) is the conditional distribution of the outcome sampled with the Best-of-N sampling. We can derive PBoN​(y∣x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x) in terms of score quantiles.

4.1.

Assuming that there is no tie in reward score, for any context xx and outcome yy, the probability mass of PBoNP_{\text{BoN}} is given by

PBoN​(y∣x)=F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)NP_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)=F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N} (6)

Positive-negative conditional independence under PBIP_{\text{BI}} is useful because Pukdee et al. (2026) showed that it is exactly the condition under which the induced pairwise preference admits a Bradley–Terry representation. In other words, the BT form is not merely a modeling assumption here, but the true functional form of PrBI⁡(y≻y′∣x)\Pr_{\text{BI}}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x), the conditional probability of preferring yy over y′y^{\prime} given xx:

PrBI⁡(y≻y′∣x):=PBI​(x,y,y′)PBI​(x,y,y′)+PBI​(x,y′,y)=σ⁡(rBI∗​(x,y)−rBI∗​(x,y′))\Pr_{\text{BI}}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x):=\frac{P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})+P_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime},y)}=\sigma(r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime})) (7)

when rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} is the population minimizer. Pukdee et al. (2026) also showed that the minimizer is given by the log ratio between the distribution of the chosen and rejected responses. These results allow us to characterize the target reward function rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} under PBIP_{\text{BI}}.

4.2Identification of rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}}.

Let rBI∗∈arg⁡minr​ℒPBI​(r)r^{*}_{\text{BI}}\in\arg\min_{r}\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BI}}}(r) then there exists a function c:𝒳→ℝc:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} such that

rBI∗​(x,y)=log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)+c⁡(x)r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)=\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}+c(x) (8)

for almost every pair (x,y)(x,y) with respect to PBIP_{\text{BI}}. Furthermore, rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} preserves the ranking induced by r∗r^{*} that is for any x,y,y′x,y,y^{\prime} with non-zero probability mass,

r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)⟹rBI∗​(x,y)>rBI∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})\implies r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)>r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime}) (9)

In other words, even though we never observe r∗r^{*}, minimizing the BT loss on BoN data recovers a reward function that agrees with r∗r^{*} on every pairwise comparison. Similarly, for the Best-vs-Worst-Independent, by conditional independence, we can also factorize the distribution PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} as

PBWI​(x,y+,y−)=P⁡(x)​PBoN​(y+∣x)​PWoN​(y−∣x)P_{\text{BWI}}(x,y^{+},y^{-})=P(x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{+}\mid x)P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{-}\mid x) (10)

and derive a similar characterization for rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}.

4.3.

Assume that there is no tie in reward score, for any context xx and outcome yy, the probability mass of PWoNP_{\text{WoN}} is given by

PWoN​(y∣x)=(1−F−​(x,y))N−(1−F⁡(x,y))NP_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)=(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N}-(1-F(x,y))^{N} (11)
4.4Identification of rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}.

Let rBWI∗∈arg⁡minr​ℒPBWI​(r)r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}\in\arg\min_{r}\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BWI}}}(r) then there exists a function c:𝒳→ℝc:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} such that

rBWI∗​(x,y)=log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)PWoN​(y∣x)+c⁡(x)r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}(x,y)=\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)}+c(x) (12)

for almost every pair (x,y)(x,y). Furthermore, rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} preserves the ranking induced by r∗r^{*} that is for any x,y,y′x,y,y^{\prime} with non-zero probability mass,

r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)⟹rBWI∗​(x,y)>rBWI∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})\implies r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}(x,y)>r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}(x,y^{\prime}) (13)

4.2 Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst

Next, we turn to the Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst scenarios where the chosen outcome and rejected outcome are no longer independent. Without independence, we show that the population risk minimizer with respect to PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBWP_{\text{BW}} does not have a closed-form minimizer anymore. We introduce a notion of comparison distribution to help with the analysis. This captures how often a pair of outcomes are compared together for a given context, regardless of which is preferred.

4.5Comparison distribution.

For any distribution PP over 𝒳×𝒴×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}, the comparison distribution P~\widetilde{P} is a distribution over xx and an unordered pair {y,y′}\{y,y^{\prime}\} with y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime} with density

P~​(x,{y,y′})∝P⁡(x,y,y′)+P⁡(x,y′,y)\widetilde{P}(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\})\propto P(x,y,y^{\prime})+P(x,y^{\prime},y) (14)
4.6Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst perform pairwise margin maximization.

Assume that there is no tie in reward score. For each context and pair of outcomes (x,{y,y′})(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\}), define

ymax∈arg⁡maxu∈{y,y′}​r∗​(x,u),ymin∈arg⁡minu∈{y,y′}​r∗​(x,u)y_{\max}\in\arg\max_{u\in\{y,y^{\prime}\}}r^{*}(x,u),\qquad y_{\min}\in\arg\min_{u\in\{y,y^{\prime}\}}r^{*}(x,u)

Then for any hypothesis class ℋ\mathcal{H}, the population risk minimizer rBR∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​ℒPBR​(r)r^{*}_{\text{BR}}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r) satisfies

rBR∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​𝔼(x,{y,y′})∼P~BR​[−log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,ymax)−r⁡(x,ymin))]r^{*}_{\text{BR}}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\})\sim\widetilde{P}_{\mathrm{BR}}}\Big[-\log\sigma\!\big(r(x,y_{\max})-r(x,y_{\min})\big)\Big]

The same result holds for rBW∗r^{*}_{\text{BW}} by replacing the comparison distribution P~BR\widetilde{P}_{\mathrm{BR}} with P~BW\widetilde{P}_{\mathrm{BW}}. In particular, both objectives are the same pairwise margin-maximization loss, differing only in the comparison distribution.

The proposition shows that for any pair of outcomes ({y,y′})(\{y,y^{\prime}\}), the BT objective maximizes the margin between the outcomes with higher and lower true reward scores. As a result, if ℋ\mathcal{H} is unbounded, then we can decrease the BT objective by increasing the margin on any pair indefinitely, Δr​(x,ymax,ymin)→∞\Delta_{r}(x,y_{\max},y_{\min})\to\infty, which leads to an unbounded minimizer. As such, we do not have a nice closed-form minimizer for rBR∗r^{*}_{\text{BR}} and rBW∗r^{*}_{\text{BW}}, and the minimizer depends on properties of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Regardless, we can still show that rBR∗→rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BR}}\to r^{*}_{\text{BI}} and rBW∗→rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BW}}\to r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} in margin semi-norm as NN grows.

4.7Margin semi-norm.

For a preference distribution PP, the margin semi-norm between two reward functions r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} is defined as

∥r1−r2∥Δ,P=𝔼(x,y,y′)∼P​[(Δr1−Δr2)2]\lVert r_{1}-r_{2}\rVert_{\Delta,P}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y,y^{\prime})\sim P}\left[(\Delta_{r_{1}}-\Delta_{r_{2}})^{2}\right] (15)
4.8rBR∗r^{*}_{\text{BR}} is close to rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}}.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a convex hypothesis class that is bounded by some constant BB. Let rBR∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​ℒPBR​(r)r^{*}_{\text{BR}}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r) then there exists a constant cBc_{B} such that for any N≥2N\geq 2,

∥rBR∗−rBI∗∥Δ,PBR≤cBN−1\lVert r^{*}_{\text{BR}}-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}\rVert_{\Delta,P_{\text{BR}}}\leq\frac{c_{B}}{N-1} (16)
4.9rBW∗r^{*}_{\text{BW}} is close to rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a convex hypothesis class that is bounded by some constant BB. Let rBW∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​ℒPBW​(r)r^{*}_{\text{BW}}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BW}}}(r) then there exists a constant cBc_{B} and ρ<1\rho<1 such that for any N≥2N\geq 2,

∥rBW∗−rBWI∗∥Δ,PBW≤cB​ρN\lVert r^{*}_{\text{BW}}-r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}\rVert_{\Delta,P_{\text{BW}}}\leq c_{B}\rho^{N} (17)

The key step in the proof is to show that PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBWP_{\text{BW}} are close in total variation distance to PBIP_{\text{BI}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}, respectively. Establishing this requires deriving closed-form expressions for the probability mass functions of these distributions and then carrying out careful algebraic comparisons; this is the most technically involved part of the argument. The convexity of ℋ\mathcal{H} is then used only to transfer this distributional closeness to closeness of the corresponding population minimizers, via a standard argument from learning theory. We defer the full proof to Appendix A.

These results imply that, as NN grows, the margins induced by rBR∗r^{*}_{\text{BR}} and rBW∗r^{*}_{\text{BW}} become close to those induced by rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} and rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}, respectively. Since rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} and rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} achieve perfect accuracy, and since the ranking is determined by the sign of the margin, it follows that the Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst settings also approximately recover the ranking induced by r∗r^{*}. Having identified these as sensible population targets, we turn to the finite-sample setting, where a fundamental tradeoff emerges: increasing NN helps in one way, but hurts in another.

Remark: Unlike the independent variants, the pairwise preferences induced by PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBWP_{\text{BW}} do not admit a BT form. However, the TV bounds above imply they approach those of the independent variants as NN grows, making BT an increasingly reasonable model.

5 Sample Complexity

In practice, we only have access to a finite number of triplets, so even if the population risk minimizer is a good target, we must also ask how quickly we can learn it. We measure the performance of the learned reward in terms of the consistency of ordering with respect to the target reward function. We define the accuracy as follows.

5.1Accuracy.

Let QQ be a test distribution over 𝒳×𝒴×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}. The accuracy of a reward function rr with respect to QQ and r∗r^{*} is given by

AccQ(r)=Prx,y,y′∼Q[sign(Δr(x,y,y′))=sign(Δr∗(x,y,y′))]\operatorname{Acc}_{Q}(r)=\Pr_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y,y^{\prime}\sim Q\end{subarray}}[\operatorname{sign}(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))=\operatorname{sign}(\Delta_{r^{*}}(x,y,y^{\prime}))] (18)

Here, we fix the test distribution QQ to represent the downstream quantity of interest, while varying the training distribution PP, which depends on NN and the base distribution PbaseP_{\text{base}}. This lets us assess the impact of the BoN preference distribution. We will focus on the Best-vs-Independent and Best-vs-Worst-Independent scenarios since they have clean target reward functions under BoN preference data (rBI∗,rBWI∗)(r^{*}_{\text{BI}},r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}) which preserve the ranking as r∗r^{*}. With finite samples, the learned reward r^\hat{r} deviates from the target due to estimation error, and whether this error flips the ranking on a given pair depends on whether it exceeds the margin between them. Pukdee et al. (2026) formalized this intuition and showed that sample complexity is governed by two quantities: the margin and the connectivity of the comparison distribution. A larger margin between two pairs of outcomes implies that the correct ordering can tolerate a larger estimation error, and a larger connectivity leads to a smaller estimation error. We analyze how the BoN preference data shapes both quantities.

5.1 Margin

First, we derive the margin of rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} and rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} and show that they grow linearly with NN.

5.2Margin of rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}}.

Assuming no ties in reward score, for any context xx and pair of outcomes y,y′y,y^{\prime} with non-zero probability mass, the margin of rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} admits the decomposition

ΔrBI∗​(x,y,y′)=N​log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)+BN​(x,y,y′),\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(x;y,y^{\prime})~=~N\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}~+~B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}), (19)

where BN​(x,y,y′)B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}) is uniformly bounded in NN.

5.3Margin of rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}.

Assume no ties in r∗​(x,⋅)r^{*}(x,\cdot). For any context xx and pair of outcomes y,y′y,y^{\prime} with non-zero probability mass, the margin of rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} admits the decomposition

ΔrBWI∗​(x,y,y′)=N⁡(log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)+log⁡1−F−​(x,y′)1−F−​(x,y))+BN​(x,y,y′)\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BWI}}}(x;y,y^{\prime})=N\left(\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}+\log\frac{1-F^{-}(x,y^{\prime})}{1-F^{-}(x,y)}\right)+B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}) (20)

where BN​(x,y,y′)B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}) is uniformly bounded in NN.

The most immediate implication is that increasing NN amplifies all pairwise margins uniformly, making it a straightforward way to make the target reward easier to learn. But the slope at which the margin grows reveals a more informative and targeted lever. The slope increases when the base distribution places more mass between the two outcomes in the reward ranking (Figure 1). We define this quantity as the between mass.

5.4Between Mass.

For any context xx and outcomes y,y′y,y^{\prime} where r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}), the between mass between yy and y′y^{\prime} is given by

Pry~∼Pbase(⋅∣x)(r∗(x,y′)<r∗(x,y~)<r∗(x,y))=F(x,y)−F(x,y′)\Pr_{\tilde{y}\sim P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x)}(r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})<r^{*}(x,\tilde{y})<r^{*}(x,y))=F(x,y)-F(x,y^{\prime}) (21)

The higher the between mass between a pair of outcomes, the faster the margin between them grows with NN.

So far, we have treated PbaseP_{\text{base}} as fixed and studied how NN shapes the induced reward. The margin decomposition reveals a complementary lever: the base distribution itself enters the margin through the between-mass term. Unlike increasing NN, which raises all margins indiscriminately, shaping PbaseP_{\text{base}} allows one to selectively increase margins on specific pairs. This lever is available whenever the practitioner has some control over the generation distribution. For example, by choosing which model to sample from or applying filtering before BoN. This selectivity is appealing because, in practice, not all pairwise comparisons are equally important: in safety, comparisons that matter most are between harmful and acceptable outputs, in reasoning, the crucial distinctions are between correct solutions and plausible near-misses. Each setting induces a different test distribution, and our result provides a principled guide for designing the base distribution to increase margins precisely where they are needed. Concretely, we provide examples of how to design the base distribution to increase margins for three different applications for reward learning.

Designing the Base Distribution to Increase Margins
Safety.

The key comparisons are those that separate harmful responses from acceptable ones. To enlarge these margins, the base distribution should place substantial mass in the mediocre region: responses that are flawed or suboptimal, but not obviously dangerous. This creates more separation between harmful and acceptable behavior.

Reasoning.

The critical distinction is between plausible-but-incorrect solutions and fully correct ones. If the base distribution produces too many clearly poor responses, then little mass lies between plausible and correct solutions. On the other hand, if it almost always produces perfect solutions, then this intermediate region again becomes small. Thus, the base distribution should be strong enough to reliably generate decent responses, while still concentrating substantial mass on near-correct but imperfect solutions.

General.

These tasks require distinguishing among responses across a broad mid-to-high quality range. Since the relevant comparisons are distributed over a wider band, the base distribution should spread its mass throughout this region in order to preserve sufficient between-mass across many comparisons.

5.2 Connectivity

Recall from Pukdee et al. (2026), the connectivity degree controls the estimation error of the reward learned from a training preference data distribution PP on a test distribution QQ in the worst-case scenario. It is defined as follows,

5.5Connectivity.

The connectivity degree of a comparison distribution PP with respect to a hypothesis class ℋ\mathcal{H} and a test distribution QQ is defined as

λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)=inff,g∈ℋ𝔼P​[(Δ​f−Δ​g)2]𝔼Q​[(Δ​f−Δ​g)2]\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})=\inf_{f,g\in\mathcal{H}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P}[(\Delta f-\Delta g)^{2}]}{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta f-\Delta g)^{2}]} (22)

The original notion of connectivity degree corresponds to the case where the test distribution QQ ranges over all comparisons in the outcome space, so that it measures how well the training distribution PP captures the pairwise variation over the entire comparison space. Here, we generalize this notion by allowing QQ to be an arbitrary, possibly selective test distribution. In this sense, λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H}) can also be interpreted as worst-case measure of how well PP covers the pairwise variation that matters under QQ.

In contrast to the margin that grows linearly with NN, we show that connectivity for PBIP_{\text{BI}} operates on an exponentially small scale in NN. The intuition is that as NN increases, BoN sampling concentrates on outcomes with extremely high rewards while WoN sampling concentrates on outcomes with extremely low rewards. As a result, the observed comparisons become increasingly concentrated on a small subset of pairs, rather than covering a broad range of pairwise comparisons. Figure 2 illustrates this in a simple finite-outcome setting, where edge thickness represents the probability of observing each comparison. As NN increases, the Best-vs-Independent graph converges to a star graph, while the Best-vs-Worst-Independent graph converges to a single edge between the best and worst outcomes. This loss of comparison diversity leaves intermediate comparisons underrepresented, which in turn degrades connectivity with respect to the test distribution QQ.

5.6Informal connectivity bounds for PBIP_{\text{BI}}.

Let PbaseP_{\text{base}} be a base distribution. For any α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and define Ax,α={y∈𝒴:r∗​(x,y)≤α}A_{x,\alpha}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:r^{*}(x,y)\leq\alpha\} as a set of outcomes which the reward is less than α\alpha for a given context xx. If ℋ\mathcal{H} is expressive enough and QQ satisfies coverage and nondegeneracy conditions, there exist constants CQ,DQ,α>0C_{Q},D_{Q,\alpha}>0 such that for any NN,

CQ​(minx,y⁡Pbase​(y∣x))N≤λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)≤DQ,α​𝔼x∼Px​[Pbase​(Ax,α∣x)N+Pbase​(Ax,α∣x)].C_{Q}\Big(\min_{x,y}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)\Big)^{N}\leq\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\leq D_{Q,\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}\!\left[P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)^{N}+P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)\right].

Thus, the connectivity degree for PBIP_{\text{BI}} is controlled by an exponentially small term in NN, together with a residual term determined by the mass of the cut Ax,αA_{x,\alpha}.

Overall, large NN can reduce connectivity by concentrating probability mass on a narrower set of comparisons. The full formal statement and proof, along with a similar result for PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}, are given in Appendix B.

5.3 Accuracy Bound

From previous sections, NN is a single knob that controls both margin and connectivity degree. However, there is a trade-off, increasing NN leads to a larger margin but decreases the connectivity degree. To make this trade-off explicit, we combine the two results into an accuracy bound that yields a practical guideline for choosing NN as a function of the sample size nn.

5.7Accuracy Bound.

Assume that ℋ\mathcal{H} is convex, bounded by some constant BB, and realizable, rBI∗∈ℋr^{*}_{\text{BI}}\in\mathcal{H}. Assume also that for every triplet (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}) in the support of QQ, both Pbase​(y∣x)P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x) and Pbase​(y′∣x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x) are non-zero. Let r^\hat{r} be the empirical risk minimizer of the BT learning objective with respect to PBIP_{\text{BI}}. Then there exist constants D>0D>0 and MQ>0M_{Q}>0 such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

AccQ⁡(r^)≥supk>0[PrQ⁡(|log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)|≥k+MQN)−D​Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)N2​k2​λconn]\operatorname{Acc}_{Q}(\hat{r})\geq\sup_{k>0}\Big[\Pr_{Q}\left(\left|\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}\right|\geq k+\frac{M_{Q}}{N}\right)\;-\;D\frac{\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta)}{N^{2}k^{2}\lambda_{\text{conn}}}\Big] (23)

where λconn:=λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)\lambda_{\text{conn}}:=\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H}).

The complexity term Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta) is a standard Rademacher-complexity quantity which we define rigorously in Appendix B. The first term measures how often the absolute margin slope under QQ exceeds a threshold, up to a vanishing O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) correction. In contrast, the second term captures the estimation error and decays like 1/(N2​λconn)1/(N^{2}\lambda_{\text{conn}}). The bound therefore preserves the same interpretation: increasing NN helps by enlarging the target margin, but hurts through the connectivity degree. The optimal choice of NN depends on the sample size nn, which in turn depends on the resource bottleneck of preference label collection.

Principle for Selecting NN Based on Resource Bottlenecks
Preference Label-Limited Regime.

In many practical settings, obtaining preference labels requires human annotators, which severely limits the number of triplets nn that can be collected. In this small-nn regime, the complexity term is large, so it is often advantageous to use a larger NN. Although a larger NN increases the cost of identifying the BoN sample, the overhead can be modest in some applications: in visual tasks, selecting the best item from NN images may be relatively easy. In addition, selecting the best item among NN candidates is substantially easier than producing a full ranking, and can be done with at most ⌈log2⁡N⌉\lceil\log_{2}N\rceil pairwise comparisons via a simple tournament procedure. Thus, when human annotation is the dominant bottleneck, it is often worthwhile to spend more effort per comparison triplet in order to improve the quality of each comparison.

Generation-Limited Regime.

When preference annotations are cheap or can be automated, for example with LLM judges, it becomes possible to collect many triplets. In this large-nn regime, increasing NN provides diminishing returns because the complexity term is already small. It is therefore more compute-efficient to use a smaller NN and spend the saved generation budget on collecting more triplets, rather than on generating many candidates for each triplet.

6 Experiments

We validate our theoretical findings on synthetic data and real-world data. We provide a brief overview of the experiment setup and results in the main text. For full details, please refer to the Appendix C.

6.1 The optimal choice of NN depends on the sample size nn.

Our theory identifies NN as a single knob that controls both margin and connectivity degree; a larger NN increases the margin but also hurts the connectivity. Our design principle suggests that we should select NN based on the sample size nn. A larger NN can help when nn is small but when nn is large, a smaller NN can become preferable.

6.1.1 Synthetic Data

Setup.

We first validate this on a synthetic dataset following the setup in Pukdee et al. (2026). In this setup, the ground-truth reward function is a cosine similarity between two embedding vectors where this embedding is an output of a two-layer neural network. We generate the training data by sampling nn triplets from the Best-vs-Independent setting and use it to train the reward model. Here, both base distribution and test distribution are uniform over the outcome space.

Results.

Figure 3 confirms the predicted tradeoff between margin and connectivity. When nn is small, larger NN achieves higher accuracy; as nn increases, the optimal NN decreases. For sufficiently large nn, smaller NN not only catches up to larger NN but can outperform it. In particular, for n≥8192n\geq 8192, N=2N=2 matches or exceeds larger NN, with a gap of up to 10 percent over N=8N=8 at n=131072n=131072. This is the regime where the loss in connectivity from larger NN outweighs its margin benefit. We also plot the connectivity degree for each NN, and additional Best-vs-Worst-Independent results in Appendix C.5. The connectivity degree decreases as NN increases and the Best-vs-Worst-Independent setting shows the same pattern.

6.1.2 Real-world Data

Setup.

We use prompts from UltraFeedback (Cui et al., 2024) as contexts xx, and generate responses with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) under Best-vs-Random and Best-vs-Worst sampling. We use Skywork-Reward-V2 (Liu et al., 2025) as the target reward function, and evaluate on a binarized UltraFeedback test set whose preference labels follow this reward. The learned reward model is a sequence classifier built on a frozen Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct backbone with a linear reward head.

Results.

Figure 4 supports our design principle that the optimal choice of NN depends on the sample size nn. When nn is small, larger NN yields higher accuracy. When nn is large enough, smaller NN achieves similar accuracy, allowing the saved compute to be used for generating more samples. For example, n=2048,N=16n=2048,N=16 achieves the same accuracy as n=8192,N=2n=8192,N=2, while the latter requires only half as much generation compute. In contrast to the synthetic data, we do not observe a crossover where smaller NN outperforms larger NN when nn is large. One possible explanation is that the test distribution here is not uniform over the outcome space, so connectivity may be less important than in the synthetic setting.

Additional Studies.

Appendix C.3 reports additional ablation studies. The connectivity degree decreases with NN, consistent with our theory (Figure 10). The Best-vs-Worst setting shows the same overall pattern and outperforms Best-vs-Random when nn is small, while the two perform similarly when nn is large. Across different base models, including gemma-3-12b-it (Kamath et al., 2025), Qwen3-8B (Team, 2025), and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512 (Liu et al., 2026), the same broad pattern holds, although the variance is higher in the small-nn regime.

6.2 Increasing the between mass of the base distribution can improve the accuracy.

Beyond choosing NN, our margin analysis suggests a second design principle: when the practitioner has control over the base distribution, PbaseP_{\text{base}} should place more mass between the comparisons that matter under the target test distribution. We now test whether reshaping PbaseP_{\text{base}} in this way translates into accuracy gains.

Setup.

We evaluate this design principle on 3 datasets representing safety, reasoning and general applications: PKU-SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025), a dataset of prompts paired with responses annotated for harmlessness; GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021a), a collection of grade-school math word problems; and UltraFeedback (Cui et al., 2024), a broad-coverage preference dataset spanning instruction-following, helpfulness, and honesty. Since GSM8K is not natively a preference dataset, we construct preference pairs by pairing a randomly chosen correct response against the highest-scoring incorrect one for each prompt. We refer to Appendix C.8 for more details. For each task, we reshape the base distribution by either increasing or decreasing the probability of responses whose scores fall into a chosen percentile band, allowing us to concentrate or disperse mass in different parts of the quality spectrum. The midpoint of the percentile band is parameterized by cc. We then generate Best-vs-Random preference data from the modified base distribution with N=4N=4, train a reward model using the same setup as in the previous experiments and compare test accuracy across different reshaped distributions. Full details of the upsampling/downsampling procedure and parameterization are given in Appendix C.6

Results.

Our goal is to understand whether reshaping the base distribution following our design principle can improve the accuracy. Figure 5, 6 and 7 compare the test accuracy of reward models trained from BoN preference data with reshaped base distribution against the original base distribution. Overall, the results support our prediction: increasing between mass on the comparisons that matter for a given task tends to improve accuracy.

Safety. The clearest improvement comes from upsampling lower-score responses (c=15c=15) while upsampling higher-score responses (c=85c=85) substantially hurts the accuracy. Downsampling lower-score responses also hurts accuracy. The score distributions show the same pattern: the best-performing base distribution places more mass on lower-score responses, whereas the worst-performing one shifts mass toward higher-score responses. This supports our prediction that, for safety tasks, keeping more mediocre responses in the base distribution increases between mass over the comparisons that matter, namely harmful versus acceptable outputs.

Reasoning. Downsampling medium-score responses (c=50c=50) leads to a higher accuracy while upsampling high-score responses (c=85c=85) leads to a lower accuracy. This suggests that in our setup, the useful comparisons are not between strong and very strong responses, but between plausible but incorrect responses and the correct responses. The original base distribution is already strong: generated responses are concentrated around reward score 25, while in the test distribution the rejected responses average around 15 and the chosen responses around 25 (Appendix C.8). As a result, pushing more mass toward the very top end reduces the between mass over the comparisons that matter. This pattern is consistent with our theory.

General. The key pattern is that upsampling mid-to-high score responses (c=30,50,85)(c=30,50,85) lowers accuracy, while downsampling in the same region improves the accuracy. This suggests that for this task, it is better to spread probability mass across this part of the quality range rather than concentrate it. The distribution of the reward score provides a weaker but compatible evidence: the worst-performing base distribution is slightly more peaked than the best-performing one.

7 Conclusion and Future Work

We study preference data generated by Best-of-NN sampling through the lens of reward learning. This perspective lets us characterize the reward targets induced by the data, identify the trade-off between margin and connectivity, and derive practical principles for data design. In particular, our analysis suggests choosing NN based on the resource bottleneck, and shaping the base distribution to place more mass between the comparisons that matter under the target test distribution. Several directions remain open, including understanding the small-NN regime, going beyond Bradley–Terry reward learning, and determining how these data-design effects propagate to downstream policy optimization and iterative training. More broadly, our results show that preference-data construction is not merely a collection detail: it shapes both what reward is learned and how efficiently it can be learned.

Appendix A Proofs for Characterizing the Learned Reward

In this section, we provide full proof details for results in Section 4.

See 4.1

Proof.

For a specific response yy to be selected as the Best-of-N, two conditions must hold:

  1. 1.

    At least one of the NN samples, y1,…,yNy_{1},\dots,y_{N} equals yy

  2. 2.

    No sample has score strictly greater than r∗​(x,y)r^{*}(x,y)

Since we assume that there is no tie in the reward score, the conditions are equivalent to when the highest reward score is r∗​(x,y)r^{*}(x,y) among NN samples.

PBoN​(y∣x)\displaystyle P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x) =Pr⁡(maxi⁡r∗​(x,yi)=r∗​(x,y))\displaystyle=\Pr(\max_{i}r^{*}(x,y_{i})=r^{*}(x,y)) (24)
=Pr⁡(r∗​(x,yi)≤r∗​(x,y))−Pr⁡(r∗​(x,yi)<r∗​(x,y))\displaystyle=\Pr(r^{*}(x,y_{i})\leq r^{*}(x,y))-\Pr(r^{*}(x,y_{i})<r^{*}(x,y)) (25)
=F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)N\displaystyle=F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N} (26)

The final line holds from independence between y1,…,yNy_{1},\dots,y_{N}. ∎

This Lemma resembles Lemma 2.3 of Beirami et al. (2025) which was for the BoN policy. We can provide a similar result for the Worst-of-N distribution as well. See 4.3

Proof.

Similar to the Best-of-N, the condition at which a response yy is the Worst-of-N is when the lowest score is r∗​(x,y)r^{*}(x,y) among NN samples y1,…,yNy_{1},\dots,y_{N}.

PWoN​(y∣x)\displaystyle P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x) =Pr⁡(mini⁡r∗​(x,yi)=r∗​(x,y))\displaystyle=\Pr(\min_{i}r^{*}(x,y_{i})=r^{*}(x,y)) (27)
=Pr⁡(r∗​(x,yi)≥r∗​(x,y))−Pr⁡(r∗​(x,yi)>r∗​(x,y))\displaystyle=\Pr(r^{*}(x,y_{i})\geq r^{*}(x,y))-\Pr(r^{*}(x,y_{i})>r^{*}(x,y)) (28)
=(1−F−​(x,y))N−(1−F⁡(x,y))N\displaystyle=(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N}-(1-F(x,y))^{N} (29)

∎

We introduce the definition of Conditional Preference Distribution (CPRD) from Pukdee et al. (2026) which encodes the preference information of a comparison distribution. This allows us to refer to the result from Pukdee et al. (2026) and cleanly identify the population minimizer.

A.1Conditional Preference Distribution (CPRD).

For a distribution PP over 𝒳×𝒴×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}, the conditional preference distribution (CPRD) of PP is defined on any unordered pair {y,y′}\{y,y^{\prime}\} with y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime} and x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} as follows

ωP​(y≻y′∣x)=P⁡(x,y,y′)P⁡(x,y,y′)+P⁡(x,y′,y).\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)=\frac{P(x,y,y^{\prime})}{P(x,y,y^{\prime})+P(x,y^{\prime},y)}. (30)

See 4.2

Proof.

Part 1: Show that rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} is a log ratio.

By Corollary 5.4 of Pukdee et al. (2026), when the comparison distribution satisfies the positive–negative conditional independence, the population minimizer of the BT learning objective, recovers the CPRD of the comparison distribution.

PrBI∗​(y≻y′∣x)=ωP​(y≻y′∣x)P_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)=\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x) (31)

almost everywhere with respect to PBIP_{\text{BI}} when PrBI∗​(y≻y′∣x)=σ⁡(rBI∗​(x,y)−rBI∗​(x,y′))P_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)=\sigma(r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime})) is the preference distribution induced by the score function rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}}.

In addition, by Theorem 4.4 of Pukdee et al. (2026), when the comparison distribution satisfies the positive–negative conditional independence, its CPRD is representable by a BT model where the score function is given by the log ratio,

ωP​(y≻y′∣x)=σ⁡(log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)−log⁡PBoN​(y′∣x)Pbase​(y′∣x))\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)=\sigma(\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}-\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}) (32)

Combining the two results, we can conclude that for all x,y,y′x,y,y^{\prime} with non-zero probability mass with respect to PBIP_{\text{BI}},

σ⁡(rBI∗​(x,y)−rBI∗​(x,y′))=σ⁡(log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)−log⁡PBoN​(y′∣x)Pbase​(y′∣x))\sigma(r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime}))=\sigma(\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}-\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}) (33)

Since σ\sigma is a strictly increasing function, we also have

rBI∗​(x,y)−rBI∗​(x,y′)=log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)−log⁡PBoN​(y′∣x)Pbase​(y′∣x)r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y^{\prime})=\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}-\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)} (34)

For any context xx, let y0y_{0} be a fixed outcome with a positive probability mass then for any yy

rBI∗​(x,y)=log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)+rBI∗​(x,y0)−log⁡PBoN​(y0∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)=\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}+r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y_{0})-\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y_{0}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)} (35)

Set c⁡(x)=rBI∗​(x,y0)−log⁡PBoN​(y0∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)c(x)=r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y_{0})-\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y_{0}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)} then we have

rBI∗​(x,y)=log⁡PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)+c⁡(x)r^{*}_{\text{BI}}(x,y)=\log\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}+c(x) (36)

for all yy with non-zero probability mass with respect to PBIP_{\text{BI}} as desired.

Part 2: Show that rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} preserves the ranking of r∗r^{*}.

It suffices to show that r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}) implies

PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)>PBoN​(y′∣x)Pbase​(y′∣x).\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}>\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}. (37)

By Lemma 4.1, we have

PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)=F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)NPbase​(y∣x).\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}=\frac{F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N}}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}. (38)

Using the factorization aN−bN=(a−b)​∑j=0N−1aN−1−j​bja^{N}-b^{N}=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a^{N-1-j}b^{j} and the fact that F⁡(x,y)−F−​(x,y)=Pbase​(y∣x)F(x,y)-F^{-}(x,y)=P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x) this simplifies to

PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)=∑j=0N−1F​(x,y)N−1−j​F−​(x,y)j.\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y)^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y)^{j}. (39)

Finally, by the definition of F⁡(x,y)F(x,y), we know that whenever r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}) we also have F⁡(x,y)>F⁡(x,y′)F(x,y)>F(x,y^{\prime}) and F−​(x,y)>F−​(x,y′)F^{-}(x,y)>F^{-}(x,y^{\prime}). Since PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)} can be written as a polynomial in F⁡(x,y),F−​(x,y)F(x,y),F^{-}(x,y) with positive coefficients, we can conclude that

∑j=0N−1F​(x,y)N−1−j​F−​(x,y)j>∑j=0N−1F​(x,y′)N−1−j​F−​(x,y′)j.\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y)^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y)^{j}>\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y^{\prime})^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y^{\prime})^{j}. (40)
PBoN​(y∣x)Pbase​(y∣x)>PBoN​(y′∣x)Pbase​(y′∣x)\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)}>\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)} (41)

This concludes our proof. ∎

See 4.4

Proof.

The first part follows the same idea as in the proof of Theorem 4.2 but just replace PbaseP_{\text{base}} with PWoNP_{\text{WoN}}. For the second part, we need to show that rBWI∗r^{*}_{\text{BWI}} preserves the ranking of r∗r^{*} where we will show that whenever r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}) we have

PBoN​(y∣x)PWoN​(y∣x)>PBoN​(y′∣x)PWoN​(y′∣x).\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)}>\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}. (42)

By Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.3, we have

PBoN​(y∣x)PWoN​(y∣x)=F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)N(1−F−​(x,y))N−(1−F⁡(x,y))N\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)}=\frac{F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N}}{(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N}-(1-F(x,y))^{N}} (43)

Using the factorization aN−bN=(a−b)​∑j=0N−1aN−1−j​bja^{N}-b^{N}=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a^{N-1-j}b^{j} and the fact that F⁡(x,y)−F−​(x,y)=Pbase​(y∣x)F(x,y)-F^{-}(x,y)=P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x) this simplifies to

PBoN​(y∣x)PWoN​(y∣x)=∑j=0N−1F​(x,y)N−1−j​F−​(x,y)j∑j=0N−1(1−F−​(x,y))N−1−j​(1−F⁡(x,y))j.\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)}=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y)^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y)^{j}}{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N-1-j}\,(1-F(x,y))^{j}}. (44)

Here the term (F⁡(x,y)−F−​(x,y))(F(x,y)-F^{-}(x,y)) cancels out.

By definition, r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}) implies F⁡(x,y)>F⁡(x,y′)F(x,y)>F(x,y^{\prime}) and 1−F−​(x,y)<1−F−​(x,y′)1-F^{-}(x,y)<1-F^{-}(x,y^{\prime}). Therefore, for the numerator, we have

∑j=0N−1F​(x,y)N−1−j​F−​(x,y)j>∑j=0N−1F​(x,y′)N−1−j​F−​(x,y′)j.\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y)^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y)^{j}>\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y^{\prime})^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y^{\prime})^{j}. (45)

For the denominator, we have

∑j=0N−1(1−F−​(x,y))N−1−j​(1−F⁡(x,y))j<∑j=0N−1(1−F−​(x,y′))N−1−j​(1−F⁡(x,y′))j.\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N-1-j}\,(1-F(x,y))^{j}<\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-F^{-}(x,y^{\prime}))^{N-1-j}\,(1-F(x,y^{\prime}))^{j}. (46)

Putting everything together, we can conclude that

∑j=0N−1F​(x,y)N−1−j​F−​(x,y)j∑j=0N−1(1−F−​(x,y))N−1−j​(1−F⁡(x,y))j>∑j=0N−1F​(x,y′)N−1−j​F−​(x,y′)j∑j=0N−1(1−F−​(x,y′))N−1−j​(1−F⁡(x,y′))j.\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y)^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y)^{j}}{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-F^{-}(x,y))^{N-1-j}\,(1-F(x,y))^{j}}>\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}F(x,y^{\prime})^{N-1-j}\,F^{-}(x,y^{\prime})^{j}}{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(1-F^{-}(x,y^{\prime}))^{N-1-j}\,(1-F(x,y^{\prime}))^{j}}. (47)

Finally,

PBoN​(y∣x)PWoN​(y∣x)>PBoN​(y′∣x)PWoN​(y′∣x).\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y\mid x)}>\frac{P_{\text{BoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}. (48)

This concludes our proof. ∎

See 4.6

Proof.

From Theorem 5.2 of Pukdee et al. (2026), the BT learning objective can be decomposed as the cross entropy between the CPRD and the preference distribution induced by the score function.

ℒP​(r)=C−Z​𝔼(x,{y,y′})∼P~[ωP​log⁡σ⁡(Δr)+(1−ωP)​log⁡(σ⁡(−Δr))]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)=C-Z\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\})\sim\widetilde{P}}\Big[\omega_{P}\log\sigma(\Delta_{r})+(1-\omega_{P})\log(\sigma(-\Delta_{r}))\Big] (49)

where ωP​(y≻y′∣x)\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x) is the CPRD of PP and Δr​(x,y,y′)=r⁡(x,y)−r⁡(x,y′)\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime})=r(x,y)-r(x,y^{\prime}) is the margin between two outcomes. C,ZC,Z are constants and P~\widetilde{P} is a comparison distribution induced by PP.

We claim that the CPRD of the Best-vs-Random scenario is either 0 or 1. For any context and pairs of outcomes (x,{y,y′})(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\}), let ymax∈arg⁡maxu∈{y,y′}​r∗​(x,u)y_{\max}\in\arg\max_{u\in\{y,y^{\prime}\}}r^{*}(x,u) and ymin∈arg⁡minu∈{y,y′}​r∗​(x,u)y_{\min}\in\arg\min_{u\in\{y,y^{\prime}\}}r^{*}(x,u) be the outcome with a higher and lower reward score. By the definition of Best-vs-Random, the reward score of the positive sample is always higher than the reward score of the negative sample. Therefore, we would always have ymaxy_{\max} as a positive sample and yminy_{\min} as a negative sample. Therefore, the CPRD is given by

ωPBR​(ymax≻ymin∣x)=P⁡(x,ymax,ymin)P⁡(x,ymax,ymin)+P⁡(x,ymin,ymax)=1\omega_{P_{\text{BR}}}(y_{\max}\succ y_{\min}\mid x)=\frac{P(x,y_{\max},y_{\min})}{P(x,y_{\max},y_{\min})+P(x,y_{\min},y_{\max})}=1 (50)

and

ωPBR​(ymin≻ymax∣x)=P⁡(x,ymin,ymax)P⁡(x,ymin,ymax)+P⁡(x,ymax,ymin)=0.\omega_{P_{\text{BR}}}(y_{\min}\succ y_{\max}\mid x)=\frac{P(x,y_{\min},y_{\max})}{P(x,y_{\min},y_{\max})+P(x,y_{\max},y_{\min})}=0. (51)

Substitute this back, we have

ωP​log⁡σ⁡(Δr)+(1−ωP)​log⁡(σ⁡(−Δr))=log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,ymax)−r⁡(x,ymin)).\omega_{P}\log\sigma(\Delta_{r})+(1-\omega_{P})\log(\sigma(-\Delta_{r}))=\log\sigma(r(x,y_{\max})-r(x,y_{\min})). (52)

With this result, we can conclude that the minimizer satisfies

rBR∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​𝔼(x,{y,y′})∼P~BR​[−log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,ymax)−r⁡(x,ymin))].r^{*}_{\text{BR}}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}_{(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\})\sim\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}}\Big[-\log\sigma(r(x,y_{\max})-r(x,y_{\min}))\Big]. (53)

The result also holds for Best-vs-Worst, which also guarantees that the reward score of the positive sample is always higher than the reward score of the negative sample. ∎

In the next part, we will show that the rBR∗r^{*}_{\text{BR}} would converge to the rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} as NN grows. To show this, we will first show that PBRP_{\text{BR}} would be close to PBIP_{\text{BI}} as NN increases. The intuition is that as NN is large, the random sample from the rest of outcomes would be close to drawing an independent sample from the base distribution. We start with first deriving the probability mass of PBRP_{\text{BR}}.

A.2Probability mass of PBRP_{\text{BR}}.

Assume that there is no tie in reward score, for any context xx and outcome y,y′y,y^{\prime} there exists a constant c>0c>0 for which the probability mass of PBRP_{\text{BR}} is given by

PBR​(x,y,y′)={0if ​y=y′​ or ​r∗​(x,y′)>r∗​(x,y)c​NN−1​P​(x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)​PBoN,N−1​(y∣x)otherwiseP_{\text{BR}}(x,y,y^{\prime})=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\text{ or }r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})>r^{*}(x,y)\\ \frac{cN}{N-1}P(x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)P_{\text{BoN},N-1}(y\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (54)

where PBoN,N−1P_{\text{BoN},N-1} is the probability mass of PBoNP_{\text{BoN}} with N−1N-1 draws.

Proof.

The first case is quite simple. When we see a pair y=y′y=y^{\prime}, we do not add it to the comparison distribution. Therefore, the probability mass is 0. In addition, if r∗​(x,y′)>r∗​(x,y)r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})>r^{*}(x,y), then it is not possible for yy to be preferred over y′y^{\prime} given the context xx. Therefore, the probability mass is 0 as well. For the second case, assume that y,y′y,y^{\prime} are two outcomes with r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′)r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime}) and y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime}. We can first factorize

PBR​(x,y,y′)=P⁡(x)​PBR​(y+=y,y−=y′∣x)P_{\text{BR}}(x,y,y^{\prime})=P(x)P_{\text{BR}}(y^{+}=y,y^{-}=y^{\prime}\mid x) (55)

where y+y^{+} and y−y^{-} are the positive and negative samples. To compute the second conditional probability term, we use the fact that for a given sample y1,…,yNy_{1},\dots,y_{N}, the probability of the positive sample being yy and the negative sample being y′y^{\prime} is given by

PBR(y+=y,y−=y′∣x,y1,…,yN)=1[argmaxyir∗(x,yi)=y]⋅|{i:yi=y′}|N−1.P_{\text{BR}}(y^{+}=y,y^{-}=y^{\prime}\mid x,y_{1},\dots,y_{N})=1[\arg\max_{y_{i}}r^{*}(x,y_{i})=y]\cdot\frac{|\{i:y_{i}=y^{\prime}\}|}{N-1}. (56)

The first term is an indicator function which ensures that the sample with the maximum reward score is yy while the second term is the probability that the random sample that is drawn uniformly from the rest of outcomes is y′y^{\prime} which is basically the number of outcomes that is equal to y′y^{\prime} divided by the number of remaining outcomes, N−1N-1. We can rewrite this as

PBR(y+=y,y−=y′∣x,y1,…,yN)=1N−11[argmaxyir∗(x,yi)=y]⋅∑i=1N1[yi=y′].P_{\text{BR}}(y^{+}=y,y^{-}=y^{\prime}\mid x,y_{1},\dots,y_{N})=\frac{1}{N-1}1[\arg\max_{y_{i}}r^{*}(x,y_{i})=y]\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{N}1[y_{i}=y^{\prime}]. (57)

Taking the expectation over all y1,…,yNy_{1},\dots,y_{N}, we have

PBR​(y+=y,y−=y′∣x)\displaystyle P_{\text{BR}}(y^{+}=y,y^{-}=y^{\prime}\mid x) =𝔼y1:N[PBR(y+=y,y−=y′∣x,y1,…,yN)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y_{1:N}}[P_{\text{BR}}(y^{+}=y,y^{-}=y^{\prime}\mid x,y_{1},\dots,y_{N})] (58)
=1N−1∑i=1NPry1:N(yi=y′,arg​maxyjr∗(x,yj)=y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Pr_{y_{1:N}}(y_{i}=y^{\prime},\argmax_{y_{j}}r^{*}(x,y_{j})=y) (59)
=1N−1∑i=1NPry1:N(yi=y′,arg​maxyj,j≠ir∗(x,yj)=y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Pr_{y_{1:N}}(y_{i}=y^{\prime},\argmax_{y_{j},j\neq i}r^{*}(x,y_{j})=y) (since ​r∗​(x,y)>r∗​(x,y′))\displaystyle(\text{since }r^{*}(x,y)>r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})) (60)
=1N−1​∑i=1NPryi⁡(yi=y′)​Pyj,j≠i​(arg​maxyj⁡r∗​(x,yj)=y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Pr_{y_{i}}(y_{i}=y^{\prime})P_{y_{j},j\neq i}(\argmax_{y_{j}}r^{*}(x,y_{j})=y) (by independence)\displaystyle(\text{by independence}) (61)
=NN−1Pbase(y′∣x)Py2:N(arg​maxyjr∗(x,yj)=y)\displaystyle=\frac{N}{N-1}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)P_{y_{2:N}}(\argmax_{y_{j}}r^{*}(x,y_{j})=y) (62)
=NN−1​Pbase​(y′∣x)​PBoN,N−1​(y∣x)\displaystyle=\frac{N}{N-1}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)P_{\text{BoN},N-1}(y\mid x) (63)

Finally, we note that the above result only holds when y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime}. When y=y′y=y^{\prime}, we have to replace |{i:yi=y′}|N−1\frac{|\{i:y_{i}=y^{\prime}\}|}{N-1} with |{i:yi=y′}|−1N−1\frac{|\{i:y_{i}=y^{\prime}\}|-1}{N-1} since one sample is already chosen as yy. Regardless, we don’t need to worry about such case since we will discard the pair with y=y′y=y^{\prime} and set the probability mass to 0. To ensure that the probability mass is valid, we need to scale up the probability mass of the rest by some factor cc. This concludes the proof.

∎

Before we prove that the total variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} is small, we first provide a lemma which relates the total variation between two distributions with its unnormalized probability mass.

A.3Normalization Preserves Closeness.

Let P~\widetilde{P} and Q~\widetilde{Q} be two unnormalized probability mass functions over a finite set of outcomes Ω\Omega. Let Zp:=∑x∈ΩP~​(x)Z_{p}:=\sum_{x\in\Omega}\widetilde{P}(x) and Zq:=∑x∈ΩQ~​(x)Z_{q}:=\sum_{x\in\Omega}\widetilde{Q}(x) be the normalization constants of P~\widetilde{P} and Q~\widetilde{Q} respectively with P⁡(x)=P~​(x)ZpP(x)=\frac{\widetilde{P}(x)}{Z_{p}} and Q⁡(x)=Q~​(x)ZqQ(x)=\frac{\widetilde{Q}(x)}{Z_{q}} as the normalized probability mass functions. If there exists a constant c>0c>0 such that Zp≥cZ_{p}\geq c and Zq≥cZ_{q}\geq c, then the total variation of P,QP,Q is bounded by the total variation of P~,Q~\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q},

TV⁡(P,Q)≤2c​TV⁡(P~,Q~)\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\leq\frac{2}{c}\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q}) (64)
Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that Zq≥ZpZ_{q}\geq Z_{p}. The total variation of P,QP,Q is given by

TV⁡(P,Q)\displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(P,Q) =12​∑x∈Ω|P⁡(x)−Q⁡(x)|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|P(x)-Q(x)| (65)
=12​∑x∈Ω|P~​(x)Zp−Q~​(x)Zq|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\frac{\widetilde{P}(x)}{Z_{p}}-\frac{\widetilde{Q}(x)}{Z_{q}}| (66)
≤12​∑x∈Ω|P~​(x)Zp−Q~​(x)Zp|+12​∑x∈Ω|Q~​(x)Zq−Q~​(x)Zp|\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\frac{\widetilde{P}(x)}{Z_{p}}-\frac{\widetilde{Q}(x)}{Z_{p}}|+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\frac{\widetilde{Q}(x)}{Z_{q}}-\frac{\widetilde{Q}(x)}{Z_{p}}| (67)
=1Zp​TV⁡(P~,Q~)+|Zp−Zq|2​Zp\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{p}}\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q})+\frac{|Z_{p}-Z_{q}|}{2Z_{p}} (68)

Since

12​|Zp−Zq|=12​|∑x∈ΩP~​(x)−∑x∈ΩQ~​(x)|≤12​∑x∈Ω|P~​(x)−Q~​(x)|=TV⁡(P~,Q~)\frac{1}{2}|Z_{p}-Z_{q}|=\frac{1}{2}|\sum_{x\in\Omega}\widetilde{P}(x)-\sum_{x\in\Omega}\widetilde{Q}(x)|\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\widetilde{P}(x)-\widetilde{Q}(x)|=\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q}) (69)

We have

TV⁡(P,Q)≤2Zp​TV⁡(P~,Q~)≤2c​TV⁡(P~,Q~)\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\leq\frac{2}{Z_{p}}\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q})\leq\frac{2}{c}\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P},\widetilde{Q}) (70)

∎

A.4Total Variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}}.

Assume that there is no tie in the reward score and we discard the pair with y=y′y=y^{\prime}. Then, for any base distribution PbaseP_{\text{base}}, there exists a constant c>0c>0 for which for any N≥2N\geq 2, the total variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} is given by

TV⁡(PBR,PBI)≤cN−1\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}},P_{\text{BI}})\leq\frac{c}{N-1} (71)
Proof.

For any fixed context xx and the positive outcome yy, the probability mass of PBIP_{\text{BI}} is given by

PBI​(y,y′∣x)={0if ​y=y′1ZI​PBoN​(y∣x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)otherwiseP_{\text{BI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ \frac{1}{Z_{I}}P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (72)

where ZIZ_{I} is a constant that compensates for the case when we discard the pair with y=y′y=y^{\prime}. On the other hand, the probability mass of PBRP_{\text{BR}} is given by

PBR​(y,y′∣x)={0if ​y=y′0if ​r∗​(x,y′)>r∗​(x,y)1ZR​NN−1​Pbase​(y′∣x)​PBoN,N−1​(y∣x)otherwiseP_{\text{BR}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ 0&\text{if }r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})>r^{*}(x,y)\\ \frac{1}{Z_{R}}\frac{N}{N-1}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)P_{\text{BoN},N-1}(y\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (73)

and ZRZ_{R} is also a normalization constant. To show that the total variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} is small, from Lemma A.3 it is sufficient to show that the unnormalized probability mass of these two distributions are close. Define the unnormalized probability mass of PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} as

P~BI​(y,y′∣x)={0if ​y=y′PBoN​(y∣x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)otherwise\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (74)
P~BR​(y,y′∣x)={0if ​y=y′0if ​r∗​(x,y′)>r∗​(x,y)NN−1​Pbase​(y′∣x)​PBoN,N−1​(y∣x)otherwise\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ 0&\text{if }r^{*}(x,y^{\prime})>r^{*}(x,y)\\ \frac{N}{N-1}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)P_{\text{BoN},N-1}(y\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (75)

Without loss of generality, let the set of outcomes {y1,…,ym}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{m}\} be ordered such that r∗​(x,y1)<r∗​(x,y2)<⋯<r∗​(x,ym)r^{*}(x,y_{1})<r^{*}(x,y_{2})<\dots<r^{*}(x,y_{m}). As a result, we can write

F⁡(x,yj)=F⁡(x,yj−1)+Pbase​(yj∣x)F(x,y_{j})=F(x,y_{j-1})+P_{\text{base}}(y_{j}\mid x) (76)

for any j∈{1,2,…,m}j\in\{1,2,\dots,m\} when F⁡(x,y0)=0F(x,y_{0})=0. Further, we will write Fj=F⁡(x,yj)F_{j}=F(x,y_{j}) and pj=Pbase​(yj∣x)p_{j}=P_{\text{base}}(y_{j}\mid x) for the convenience of notation. With this notation, we know that P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)=0\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)=0 for any i<ji<j since the reward score of yiy_{i} is lower than yjy_{j} so it’s not possible for yiy_{i} to be preferred over yjy_{j} under Best-vs-Random. Therefore, the total variation between P~BI\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}} and P~BR\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}} is given by

2​TV⁡(P~BI,P~BR)\displaystyle 2\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}},\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}) =∑y,y′|P~BI​(y,y′∣x)−P~BR​(y,y′∣x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{y,y^{\prime}}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)| (77)
=∑i>j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)−P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)|+∑i<j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)−P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)|+\sum_{i<j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)| (78)
=∑i>j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)−P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)|+∑i<j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)|+\sum_{i<j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)| (79)

We can split the total variation into two parts. The first part is the difference between the probability mass of P~BI\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}} and P~BR\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}} when i>ji>j while the second part is just the probability mass of P~BI\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}} when i<ji<j. We bound the first part as follows:

∑i>j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)−P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)|\displaystyle\sum_{i>j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)| =∑i>j|PBoN​(yi∣x)​Pbase​(yj∣x)−NN−1​PBoN,N−1​(yi∣x)​Pbase​(yj∣x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}|P_{\text{BoN}}(y_{i}\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y_{j}\mid x)-\frac{N}{N-1}P_{\text{BoN},N-1}(y_{i}\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y_{j}\mid x)| (80)
=∑i>j|(FiN−Fi−1N)−NN−1​(FiN−1−Fi−1N−1)|​pj\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}|(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})-\frac{N}{N-1}(F_{i}^{N-1}-F_{i-1}^{N-1})|p_{j} (81)

Let g⁡(u)=NN−1​uN−1−uNg(u)=\frac{N}{N-1}u^{N-1}-u^{N}. Differentiating g⁡(u)g(u) with respect to uu, we have g′​(u)=N​uN−2​(1−u)≥0g^{\prime}(u)=Nu^{N-2}(1-u)\geq 0 for all u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] which implies that g⁡(u)g(u) is increasing on [0,1][0,1]. We can write the term above in terms of gg,

(FiN−Fi−1N)−NN−1​(FiN−1−Fi−1N−1)=g⁡(Fi−1)−g⁡(Fi)≤0\displaystyle(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})-\frac{N}{N-1}(F_{i}^{N-1}-F_{i-1}^{N-1})=g(F_{i-1})-g(F_{i})\leq 0 (82)

This follows from the fact that g⁡(u)g(u) is increasing while Fi>Fi−1F_{i}>F_{i-1}. Therefore, we have

∑i>j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)−P~BR​(yi,yj∣x)|\displaystyle\sum_{i>j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)-\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)| =∑i>j(g⁡(Fi)−g⁡(Fi−1))​pj\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}(g(F_{i})-g(F_{i-1}))p_{j} (83)
=∑j=1m−1pj​∑i=j+1m(g⁡(Fi)−g⁡(Fi−1))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}p_{j}\sum_{i=j+1}^{m}(g(F_{i})-g(F_{i-1})) (84)
=∑j=1m−1pj​(g⁡(Fm)−g⁡(Fj))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}p_{j}(g(F_{m})-g(F_{j})) (85)
≤∑j=1m−1pj​g​(Fm)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}p_{j}g(F_{m}) (86)
≤g⁡(Fm)=g⁡(1)=1N−1\displaystyle\leq g(F_{m})=g(1)=\frac{1}{N-1} (87)

For the second part, we have

∑i<j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)|\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)| =∑i<j(FiN−Fi−1N)​pj\displaystyle=\sum_{i<j}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})p_{j} (88)
=∑i=1m−1∑j=i+1m(FiN−Fi−1N)​pj\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})p_{j} (89)
=∑i=1m(FiN−Fi−1N)​∑j=i+1mpj\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}p_{j} (90)
=∑i=1m−1(FiN−Fi−1N)​(1−Fi)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})(1-F_{i}) (91)
=∑i=1m−1FiN−Fi−1N−FiN+1+Fi​Fi−1N\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N}-F_{i}^{N+1}+F_{i}F_{i-1}^{N} (92)
=Fm−1N−∑i=1m−1FiN+1+∑i=1m−1(Fi−1+pi)​Fi−1N\displaystyle=F_{m-1}^{N}-\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}F_{i}^{N+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}(F_{i-1}+p_{i})F_{i-1}^{N} (93)
=Fm−1N−∑i=1m−1FiN+1+∑i=0m−2FiN+1+∑i=1m−1pi​Fi−1N\displaystyle=F_{m-1}^{N}-\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}F_{i}^{N+1}+\sum_{i=0}^{m-2}F_{i}^{N+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}p_{i}F_{i-1}^{N} (94)
=Fm−1N−Fm−1N+1+∑i=1m−1pi​Fi−1N\displaystyle=F_{m-1}^{N}-F_{m-1}^{N+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}p_{i}F_{i-1}^{N} (95)
=Fm−1N​(1−Fm−1)+∑i=1m−1pi​Fi−1N\displaystyle=F_{m-1}^{N}(1-F_{m-1})+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}p_{i}F_{i-1}^{N} (96)
=∑i=1mpi​Fi−1N\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}F_{i-1}^{N} (97)

Here we use the telescoping technique. We observe that the third term is a left Riemann sum for approximating the integral of uNu^{N} between 00 and 11 by splitting [0,1][0,1] into intervals with width p1,p2,…,pm−1,pmp_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{m-1},p_{m}. Since this function is increasing, we can conclude that the Riemann sum is upper bounded by the true integral.

∑i=1mFi−1N​pi≤∫01uN​𝑑u=1N+1\sum_{i=1}^{m}F_{i-1}^{N}p_{i}\leq\int_{0}^{1}u^{N}du=\frac{1}{N+1} (98)

Therefore,

∑i<j|P~BI​(yi,yj∣x)|≤1N+1\sum_{i<j}|\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)|\leq\frac{1}{N+1} (99)

Combining two parts, we can conclude that

2​TV⁡(P~BI,P~BR)≤1N−1+1N+1≤2N−12\operatorname{TV}(\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}},\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}})\leq\frac{1}{N-1}+\frac{1}{N+1}\leq\frac{2}{N-1} (100)

The final step we need is to show that the normalization constant of PBIP_{\text{BI}} and PBRP_{\text{BR}} are bounded below by a constant. We start with ZIZ_{I}.

ZI\displaystyle Z_{I} =∑i≠jP~BI​(yi,yj∣x)\displaystyle=\sum_{i\neq j}\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x) (101)
=1−∑i=1mP~BI​(yi,yi∣x)\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\widetilde{P}_{\text{BI}}(y_{i},y_{i}\mid x) (102)
