ZIZ_{I} is bounded below by 1−max⁡pi1-\max p_{i} for any NN. In addition, for ZRZ_{R}, we have

ZR\displaystyle Z_{R} =∑i>jP~BR​(yi,yj∣x)\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}\widetilde{P}_{\text{BR}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x) (105)
=∑i>jNN−1​(FiN−1−Fi−1N−1)​pj\displaystyle=\sum_{i>j}\frac{N}{N-1}(F_{i}^{N-1}-F_{i-1}^{N-1})p_{j} (106)
≥NN−1​(FmN−1−Fm−1N−1)​pm\displaystyle\geq\frac{N}{N-1}(F_{m}^{N-1}-F_{m-1}^{N-1})p_{m} (107)
=NN−1​(1−(1−pm)N−1)​pm\displaystyle=\frac{N}{N-1}(1-(1-p_{m})^{N-1})p_{m} (108)
≥pm2\displaystyle\geq p_{m}^{2} (109)

The lower bound here is fairly loose but it is sufficient for us to use Lemma A.3 which now implies that there exists a constant cx>0c_{x}>0 such that

TV⁡(PBR​(y,y′∣x),PBI​(y,y′∣x))≤cxN−1\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x),P_{\text{BI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x))\leq\frac{c_{x}}{N-1} (110)

for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. Now, we take the summation over all xx and will have the total variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} is bounded by

TV⁡(PBR,PBI)=∑xP⁡(x)​TV⁡(PBR​(y,y′∣x),PBI​(y,y′∣x))≤cN−1\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}},P_{\text{BI}})=\sum_{x}P(x)\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x),P_{\text{BI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x))\leq\frac{c}{N-1} (111)

when c=∑xP⁡(x)​cxc=\sum_{x}P(x)c_{x}. This concludes the proof.

∎

Now, we have established that PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} are close as NN grows, with this we can also show that the population risk minimizer would also be close to each other as well. Here we apply a standard technique in learning theory that first shows that a small TV distance means that the difference in the population risk would be small. Then, we use the strong convexity of the population risk to show that the difference in the population risk minimizer would be small as well. We will first prove some technical lemmas that will be useful for the proof and then will present the main proof accordingly.

The first lemma shows that we can bound the population risk difference in terms of the total variation between the two distributions.

A.5.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a hypothesis class that is bounded by some constant BB. Let PP and QQ be two comparison distributions then there exists a constant MBM_{B} such that

supr∈ℋ|ℒP​(r)−ℒQ​(r)|≤2​MB​TV⁡(P,Q)\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r)|\leq 2M_{B}\operatorname{TV}(P,Q) (112)
Proof.

First, we will show that if ℋ\mathcal{H} is bounded by BB then the BT loss is also bounded as well. Recall that the loss on any (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}) is given by

ℓ⁡(Δr)=−log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,y+)−r⁡(x,y−))=log⁡(1+exp⁡(r⁡(x,y−)−r⁡(x,y+))).\ell(\Delta_{r})=-\log\sigma(r(x,y^{+})-r(x,y^{-}))=\log(1+\exp(r(x,y^{-})-r(x,y^{+}))). (113)

Since rr is bounded by BB, we have |r⁡(x,y−)−r⁡(x,y+)|≤2​B|r(x,y^{-})-r(x,y^{+})|\leq 2B so that

ℓ⁡(Δr)≤log⁡(1+exp⁡(2​B)):=MB.\ell(\Delta_{r})\leq\log(1+\exp(2B)):=M_{B}. (114)

Next, we will show that the difference in the population risk is bounded by the total variation between the two distributions.

|ℒP​(r)−ℒQ​(r)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r)| =|∑x,y,y′P⁡(x,y,y′)​ℓ​(Δr​(x,y,y′))−∑x,y,y′Q⁡(x,y,y′)​ℓ​(Δr​(x,y,y′))|\displaystyle=|\sum_{x,y,y^{\prime}}P(x,y,y^{\prime})\ell(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))-\sum_{x,y,y^{\prime}}Q(x,y,y^{\prime})\ell(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))| (115)
=|∑x,y,y′(P⁡(x,y,y′)−Q⁡(x,y,y′))​ℓ​(Δr​(x,y,y′))|\displaystyle=|\sum_{x,y,y^{\prime}}(P(x,y,y^{\prime})-Q(x,y,y^{\prime}))\ell(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))| (116)
≤∑x,y,y′|P(x,y,y′)−Q(x,y,y′)|ℓ(Δr(x,y,y′))|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x,y,y^{\prime}}|P(x,y,y^{\prime})-Q(x,y,y^{\prime})|\ell(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))| (117)
≤∑x,y,y′|P⁡(x,y,y′)−Q⁡(x,y,y′)|​MB\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x,y,y^{\prime}}|P(x,y,y^{\prime})-Q(x,y,y^{\prime})|M_{B} (118)
=2​MB​TV⁡(P,Q)\displaystyle=2M_{B}\operatorname{TV}(P,Q) (119)

Since this is true for any r∈ℋr\in\mathcal{H}, it would also hold for the supremum over all r∈ℋr\in\mathcal{H}. This concludes the proof. ∎

The second lemma shows that if the population risk between two distributions is small on all hypotheses in the hypothesis class, then the population risk minimizer of one distribution would also perform well on the other distribution.

A.6.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a hypothesis class and PP, QQ be two comparison distributions such that supr∈ℋ|ℒP​(r)−ℒQ​(r)|≤ϵ\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r)|\leq\epsilon. Let rP∗r^{*}_{P} and rQ∗r^{*}_{Q} be the population risk minimizer of ℒP\mathcal{L}_{P} and ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q} respectively. Then, we have

ℒP​(rQ∗)≤ℒP​(rP∗)+2​ϵ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{Q})\leq\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})+2\epsilon (120)
ℒQ​(rP∗)≤ℒQ​(rQ∗)+2​ϵ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{P})\leq\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q})+2\epsilon (121)
Proof.

We write the difference between the population risk of rP∗r^{*}_{P} and rQ∗r^{*}_{Q} as

ℒP​(rQ∗)−ℒP​(rP∗)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{Q})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P}) =(ℒP​(rQ∗)−ℒQ​(rQ∗))+(ℒQ​(rQ∗)−ℒQ​(rP∗))+(ℒQ​(rP∗)−ℒP​(rP∗))\displaystyle=(\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{Q})-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q}))+(\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q})-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{P}))+(\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{P})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})) (122)
≤|ℒP​(rQ∗)−ℒQ​(rQ∗)|+(ℒQ​(rQ∗)−ℒQ​(rP∗))+|ℒQ​(rP∗)−ℒP​(rP∗)|\displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{Q})-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q})|+(\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q})-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{P}))+|\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{P})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})| (123)
≤ϵ+0+ϵ=2​ϵ\displaystyle\leq\epsilon+0+\epsilon=2\epsilon (124)

The first and third term follows from the assumption that supr∈ℋ|ℒP​(r)−ℒQ​(r)|≤ϵ\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r)|\leq\epsilon. The second term is at most 0 since rQ∗r^{*}_{Q} is the population risk minimizer of ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q} so that ℒQ​(rQ∗)≤ℒQ​(r)\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r^{*}_{Q})\leq\mathcal{L}_{Q}(r) for any r∈ℋr\in\mathcal{H} including rP∗r^{*}_{P}. We have the first result and the second result follows from the same argument. ∎

In this Lemma, we show that when the hypothesis class is convex, we can bound the difference between the margin of a reward function with the population risk minimizer with the difference in their population risk.

A.7.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a convex hypothesis class that is bounded by some constant BB. Let PP be a comparison distribution and rP∗r^{*}_{P} be the population risk minimizer of ℒP\mathcal{L}_{P}. There exists a constant cBc_{B} such that for any reward function r∈ℋr\in\mathcal{H}, we have

∥r−rP∗∥Δ,P≤2σB​(ℒP​(r)−ℒP​(rP∗))\lVert r-r^{*}_{P}\rVert_{\Delta,P}\leq\frac{2}{\sigma_{B}}(\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})) (125)
Proof.

First, we will show that when ℋ\mathcal{H} is bounded, ℒP​(r)\mathcal{L}_{P}(r) is strongly convex. This result follows from the proof of Theorem 6.7 in Pukdee et al. (2026). We provide a brief proof here for completeness. We can write the BT objective as

ℒP​(r)=C+𝔼(x,{y,y′})∼P~​[gx,y,y′​(Δr​(x,y,y′))].\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)=C+\mathbb{E}_{(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\})\sim\widetilde{P}}\left[g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}))\right]. (126)

where gx,y,y′:ℝ→ℝg_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, is defined for each (x,{y,y′})(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\}) as

gx,y,y′​(a)\displaystyle g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(a) =−ωP​(y≻y′∣x)​log⁡σ⁡(a)−(1−ωP​(y≻y′∣x))​log⁡(1−σ⁡(a))\displaystyle=-\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)\log\sigma(a)-(1-\omega_{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x))\log(1-\sigma(a)) (127)

We will write Δr\Delta_{r} for Δr​(x,y,y′)\Delta_{r}(x,y,y^{\prime}) for convenience from now. The first thing we will show is that gx,y,y′g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}} is strongly convex with respect to aa. We can check this by taking the derivative. Using the property that σ′​(a)=σ⁡(a)​(1−σ⁡(a))\sigma^{\prime}(a)=\sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a)), we have the first derivative

gx,y,y′′​(a)=σ⁡(a)−ωPg_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}^{\prime}(a)=\sigma(a)-\omega_{P} (128)

and the second derivative

gx,y,y′′′​(a)=σ⁡(a)​(1−σ⁡(a))g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}^{\prime\prime}(a)=\sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a)) (129)

Since the score function rr is bounded by a constant BB, for any (x,{y,y′})(x,\{y,y^{\prime}\}), we know that |Δr|=|r⁡(x,y)−r⁡(x,y′)|≤2​B|\Delta_{r}|=|r(x,y)-r(x,y^{\prime})|\leq 2B. Now, for a∈[−2​B,2​B]a\in[-2B,2B] we know that

σ⁡(a)​(1−σ⁡(a))≥σ⁡(2​B)​(1−σ⁡(2​B)):=σB>0\sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a))\geq\sigma(2B)(1-\sigma(2B)):=\sigma_{B}>0 (130)

With this assumption, we can conclude that gx,y,y′g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}} is σB\sigma_{B}-strongly convex. Recall that if ff is σB\sigma_{B}-strongly convex, then for any x,yx,y, we have

f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)≥f′​(y)​(x−y)+σB2​(x−y)2.f(x)-f(y)\geq f^{\prime}(y)(x-y)+\frac{\sigma_{B}}{2}(x-y)^{2}. (131)

Apply this inequality on gx,y,y′g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}} with Δr\Delta_{r} and ΔrP∗\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}} and drop (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}) for convenience.

gx,y,y′​(Δr)−gx,y,y′​(ΔrP∗)≥gx,y,y′′​(ΔrP∗)​(Δr−ΔrP∗)+σB2​(Δr−ΔrP∗)2.g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r})-g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})\geq g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})+\frac{\sigma_{B}}{2}(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}. (132)

Take the expectation over the distribution P~\widetilde{P}, we have

𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′​(Δr)−gx,y,y′​(ΔrP∗)]≥𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′′​(ΔrP∗)​(Δr−ΔrP∗)]+σB2​𝔼P~​[(Δr−ΔrP∗)2].\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r})-g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})]\geq\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})]+\frac{\sigma_{B}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]. (133)

The left hand side is just the difference between the population risk, while the second term on the right hand side is the margin semi-norm with respect to PP; since (Δr−ΔrP∗)2(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2} is invariant under swapping yy and y′y^{\prime}, its expectation under P~\widetilde{P} is equal to the expectation over PP which is exactly ∥r−rP∗∥Δ,P\lVert r-r^{*}_{P}\rVert_{\Delta,P}.

ℒP​(r)−ℒP​(rP∗)≥𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′′​(ΔrP∗)​(Δr−ΔrP∗)]+σB2​∥r−rP∗∥Δ,P.\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})\geq\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})]+\frac{\sigma_{B}}{2}\lVert r-r^{*}_{P}\rVert_{\Delta,P}. (134)

Now, the final part is to show that the first term on the right hand side is non-negative. We achieve this by using the property of ℋ\mathcal{H} being convex. From convexity, we know that for any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we have

rt=(1−t)​rP∗+t​r∈ℋr_{t}=(1-t)r^{*}_{P}+tr\in\mathcal{H} (135)

Since rP∗r^{*}_{P} is the population risk minimizer, the right derivative of the population risk with respect to tt at t=0t=0 must be non-negative.

∂∂t​ℒP​(rt)|t=0≥0\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathcal{L}_{P}(r_{t})\bigg|_{t=0}\geq 0 (136)

where

∂∂t​ℒP​(rt)\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathcal{L}_{P}(r_{t}) =∂∂t​𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′​(Δrt)]\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r_{t}})] (137)
=𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′′​(Δrt)​∂∂t​Δrt]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r_{t}})\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Delta_{r_{t}}] (138)

We can derive

∂∂t​Δrt\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Delta_{r_{t}} =∂∂t​((1−t)​ΔrP∗+t​Δr)=Δr−ΔrP∗.\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}((1-t)\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}}+t\Delta_{r})=\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}}. (139)

Therefore,

∂∂t​ℒP​(rt)=𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′′​(Δrt)​(Δr−ΔrP∗)]\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathcal{L}_{P}(r_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r_{t}})(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})] (140)

Setting t=0t=0 and substituting back, we would have that

𝔼P~​[gx,y,y′′​(ΔrP∗)​(Δr−ΔrP∗)]≥0\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}}[g^{\prime}_{x,{y,y^{\prime}}}(\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})(\Delta_{r}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})]\geq 0 (141)

as desired. As a result, we can conclude that

ℒP​(r)−ℒP​(rP∗)≥σB2​∥r−rP∗∥Δ,P.\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})\geq\frac{\sigma_{B}}{2}\lVert r-r^{*}_{P}\rVert_{\Delta,P}. (142)

This concludes the proof. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove the Theorem 4.8. See 4.8

Proof.

First, by proposition A.4, we have that the total variation between PBRP_{\text{BR}} and PBIP_{\text{BI}} is bounded by cN−1\frac{c}{N-1} for some constant c>0c>0,

TV⁡(PBR,PBI)≤cN−1.\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}},P_{\text{BI}})\leq\frac{c}{N-1}. (143)

By Lemma A.5, we can bound the population risk difference with the total variation,

supr∈ℋ|ℒPBR​(r)−ℒPBI​(r)|≤2​MB​TV⁡(PBR,PBI)≤2​MB​cN−1.\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BI}}}(r)|\leq 2M_{B}\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BR}},P_{\text{BI}})\leq\frac{2M_{B}c}{N-1}. (144)

By Lemma A.6, we would have

ℒPBR​(rBI∗)−ℒPBR​(rBR∗)≤4​MB​cN−1\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r^{*}_{\text{BI}})-\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r^{*}_{\text{BR}})\leq\frac{4M_{B}c}{N-1} (145)

Finally, by the convexity of ℋ\mathcal{H} and Lemma A.7, we have

∥rBR∗−rBI∗∥Δ,PBR≤2σB​(ℒPBR​(rBI∗)−ℒPBR​(rBR∗))≤8​MB​cσB​(N−1).\lVert r^{*}_{\text{BR}}-r^{*}_{\text{BI}}\rVert_{\Delta,P_{\text{BR}}}\leq\frac{2}{\sigma_{B}}(\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r^{*}_{\text{BI}})-\mathcal{L}_{P_{\text{BR}}}(r^{*}_{\text{BR}}))\leq\frac{8M_{B}c}{\sigma_{B}(N-1)}. (146)

Setting cB=8​MB​cσBc_{B}=\frac{8M_{B}c}{\sigma_{B}} concludes the proof. ∎

The proof for Theorem 4.9 follows the same argument. The key difference is to show that the total variation between PBWP_{\text{BW}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} now decays exponentially.

A.8Total Variation between PBWP_{\text{BW}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}.

Assume that there is no tie in the reward score and we discard the pair with y=y′y=y^{\prime}. Then, there exists a constant c>0c>0 and ρ<1\rho<1 for which for any N≥2N\geq 2, the total variation between PBWP_{\text{BW}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} is given by

TV⁡(PBW,PBWI)≤c​ρN\operatorname{TV}(P_{\text{BW}},P_{\text{BWI}})\leq c\rho^{N} (147)
Proof.

The main idea of the proof is to bound the total variation between PBWP_{\text{BW}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} on the pair of best and worst outcome. This is because we know that as NN grows, we are more likely to see the outcome with the highest and lowest true reward score. For the first step, we will calculate the probability mass of PBWP_{\text{BW}} and PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}.

Part 1: Calculate the probability mass of PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} and PBWP_{\text{BW}}. We start with the probability mass of PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}.

PBWI​(y,y′∣x)={0if ​y=y′1cI​PBoN​(y∣x)​PWoN​(y′∣x)otherwiseP_{\text{BWI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }y=y^{\prime}\\ \frac{1}{c_{I}}P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (148)

Here cIc_{I} is a constant that ensures that PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} is a valid probability distribution. We need this constant because whenever y=y′y=y^{\prime}, we discard the triplet. We will bound this constant term. Without loss of generality, assume that the set of outcomes is given by y1,y2,…,ymy_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{m} where r∗​(x,y1)<r∗​(x,y2)<⋯<r∗​(x,ym)r^{*}(x,y_{1})<r^{*}(x,y_{2})<\dots<r^{*}(x,y_{m}) so that y1y_{1} is the worst outcome and ymy_{m} is the best outcome. We also define the unnormalized probability mass of PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} as

P~BWI​(y,y′∣x)=PBoN​(y∣x)​PWoN​(y′∣x)\widetilde{P}_{\text{BWI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x)=P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x) (149)

From Lemma 4.1 and 4.3, we have

P~BWI​(yi,yj∣x)\displaystyle\widetilde{P}_{\text{BWI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x) =PBoN​(yi∣x)​PWoN​(yj∣x)\displaystyle=P_{\text{BoN}}(y_{i}\mid x)P_{\text{WoN}}(y_{j}\mid x) (150)
=(F​(x,yi)N−F−​(x,yi)N)​((1−F−​(x,yj))N−(1−F⁡(x,yj))N)\displaystyle=(F(x,y_{i})^{N}-F^{-}(x,y_{i})^{N})((1-F^{-}(x,y_{j}))^{N}-(1-F(x,y_{j}))^{N}) (151)
=(F​(x,yi)N−F​(x,yi−1)N)​((1−F⁡(x,yj−1))N−(1−F⁡(x,yj))N)\displaystyle=(F(x,y_{i})^{N}-F(x,y_{i-1})^{N})((1-F(x,y_{j-1}))^{N}-(1-F(x,y_{j}))^{N}) (152)
=(FiN−Fi−1N)​((1−Fj−1)N−(1−Fj)N)\displaystyle=(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})((1-F_{j-1})^{N}-(1-F_{j})^{N}) (153)

This follows from the fact that F−​(x,yi)=F⁡(x,yi−1)F^{-}(x,y_{i})=F(x,y_{i-1}). We also write Fi=F⁡(x,yi)F_{i}=F(x,y_{i}) for convenience. It is clear that PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} is just P~BWI\widetilde{P}_{\text{BWI}} normalized by some constant that takes care of the case when we discard the pair with y=y′y=y^{\prime}. Therefore,

cI\displaystyle c_{I} =∑y≠y′P~BWI​(y,y′∣x)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\neq y^{\prime}}\widetilde{P}_{\text{BWI}}(y,y^{\prime}\mid x) (154)
=1−∑i=1mP~BWI​(yi,yi∣x)\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\widetilde{P}_{\text{BWI}}(y_{i},y_{i}\mid x) (155)
=1−∑i=1m(FiN−Fi−1N)​((1−Fi−1)N−(1−Fi)N)\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})((1-F_{i-1})^{N}-(1-F_{i})^{N}) (156)

For each ii between 1 and mm, the term (FiN−Fi−1N)​((1−Fi−1)N−(1−Fi)N)(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})((1-F_{i-1})^{N}-(1-F_{i})^{N}) would converge to 00 as NN grows. Further, when i=1i=1, we have

(F1N−F0N)​((1−F0)N−(1−F1)N)=F1N​(1−(1−F1)N)(F_{1}^{N}-F_{0}^{N})((1-F_{0})^{N}-(1-F_{1})^{N})=F_{1}^{N}(1-(1-F_{1})^{N}) (157)

and when i=mi=m, we have

(FmN−Fm−1N)​((1−Fm−1)N−(1−Fm)N)=(1−Fm−1N)​(1−Fm−1)N(F_{m}^{N}-F_{m-1}^{N})((1-F_{m-1})^{N}-(1-F_{m})^{N})=(1-F_{m-1}^{N})(1-F_{m-1})^{N} (158)

Both terms also converge to 00 as NN grows. As a result, we can conclude that cI→1c_{I}\to 1 as NN grows and there exists a constant a>0a>0 for which cI≥a>0c_{I}\geq a>0 for all NN. Combining everything together, we have

PBWI​(yi,yj∣x)={0if ​i=j1cI​(FiN−Fi−1N)​((1−Fj−1)N−(1−Fj)N)otherwiseP_{\text{BWI}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }i=j\\ \frac{1}{c_{I}}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})((1-F_{j-1})^{N}-(1-F_{j})^{N})&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (159)

when cI→1c_{I}\to 1 as NN grows. Next, we will calculate the probability mass of PBWP_{\text{BW}}. First, for any i≤ji\leq j we know that

PBW​(yi,yj∣x)=0P_{\text{BW}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x)=0 (160)

because yjy_{j} has a higher reward score than yiy_{i} so it’s impossible for yiy_{i} to be preferred over yjy_{j}. For the case when i>ji>j, the probability is not zero anymore. Let Y1,Y2,…,YNY_{1},Y_{2},\dots,Y_{N} be the NN outcomes sampled from the base distribution and let P~BW\widetilde{P}_{\text{BW}} be the unnormalized probability mass of PBWP_{\text{BW}} then

P~BW​(yi,yj∣x)\displaystyle\widetilde{P}_{\text{BW}}(y_{i},y_{j}\mid x) =Pr⁡(arg⁡maxYi​r∗​(x,Yi)=yi,arg⁡minYi​r∗​(x,Yi)=yj)\displaystyle=\Pr(\arg\max_{Y_{i}}r^{*}(x,Y_{i})=y_{i},\arg\min_{Y_{i}}r^{*}(x,Y_{i})=y_{j}) (161)
=Pr⁡(max⁡r∗​(x,Yi)=r∗​(x,yi),min⁡r∗​(x,Yi)=r∗​(x,yj))\displaystyle=\Pr(\max r^{*}(x,Y_{i})=r^{*}(x,y_{i}),\min r^{*}(x,Y_{i})=r^{*}(x,y_{j})) (162)

=(Fi−Fj−1)N−(Fi−1−Fj−1)N−(Fi−Fj)N+(Fi−1−Fj)N\displaystyle=(F_{i}-F_{j-1})^{N}-(F_{i-1}-F_{j-1})^{N}-(F_{i}-F_{j})^{N}+(F_{i-1}-F_{j})^{N} (165)

B.1Formal connectivity bounds for PBIP_{\text{BI}}.

Assume that every triplet in the support of QQ has non-zero probability under PBIP_{\text{BI}}. Then there exists a constant CQ>0C_{Q}>0 for which for any NN,

γQ,α:=PrQ⁡(y∈Ax,α,y′∉Ax,α)+PrQ⁡(y∉Ax,α,y′∈Ax,α)>0.\gamma_{Q,\alpha}:=\Pr_{Q}(y\in A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\notin A_{x,\alpha})+\Pr_{Q}(y\notin A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\in A_{x,\alpha})>0.

If η:=1−maxx,y⁡Pbase​(y∣x)>0\eta:=1-\max_{x,y}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)>0, then there exists a constant DQ,α>0D_{Q,\alpha}>0 such that for any NN,

λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)≤DQ,α​𝔼x∼Px​[Pbase​(Ax,α∣x)N+Pbase​(Ax,α∣x)]\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\leq D_{Q,\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}[P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)^{N}+P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)] (212)
Proof.

𝔼PBI​[(Δ​f−Δ​g)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P_{\text{BI}}}[(\Delta f-\Delta g)^{2}] ≥∑Q⁡(x,y,y′)>0PBI​(x,y,y′)​(Δ​f−Δ​g)2\displaystyle\geq\sum_{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})>0}P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})(\Delta f-\Delta g)^{2} (214)

≥(minQ⁡(x,y,y′)>0⁡PBI​(x,y,y′)Q⁡(x,y,y′))​𝔼Q​[(Δ​f−Δ​g)2].\displaystyle\geq\left(\min_{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})>0}\frac{P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}\right)\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta f-\Delta g)^{2}]. (216)

Therefore,

λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)≥minQ⁡(x,y,y′)>0⁡PBI​(x,y,y′)Q⁡(x,y,y′).\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\geq\min_{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})>0}\frac{P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}. (217)

Let

≥P⁡(x)​PBoN​(y∣x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)Q⁡(x,y,y′)\displaystyle\geq\frac{P(x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})} (220)

since ZI​(x)≤1Z_{I}(x)\leq 1. By Lemma 4.1,

PBoN​(y∣x)=F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)N≥Pbase​(y∣x)N.P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)=F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N}\geq P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)^{N}. (221)

Hence, for every (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}) in the support of QQ,

PBI​(x,y,y′)Q⁡(x,y,y′)≥P⁡(x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)Q⁡(x,y,y′)​Pbase​(y∣x)N≥CQ​(minx,y⁡Pbase​(y∣x))N\frac{P_{\text{BI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}\geq\frac{P(x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)^{N}\geq C_{Q}(\min_{x,y}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x))^{N} (222)

where

CQ:=minQ⁡(x,y,y′)>0⁡P⁡(x)​Pbase​(y′∣x)Q⁡(x,y,y′)>0.C_{Q}:=\min_{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})>0}\frac{P(x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}>0. (223)

Substituting back, we obtain

λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)≥CQ​(minx,y⁡Pbase​(y∣x))N.\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\geq C_{Q}(\min_{x,y}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x))^{N}. (224)

Now, we prove the upper bound. Fix α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and define

Ax,α={y∈𝒴:r∗​(x,y)≤α}A_{x,\alpha}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:r^{*}(x,y)\leq\alpha\} (225)

and write pA​(x):=Pbase​(Ax,α∣x)p_{A}(x):=P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x). Without loss of generality, let the set of outcomes be {y1,y2,…,ym}\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{m}\} such that r∗​(x,y1)<r∗​(x,y2)<⋯<r∗​(x,ym)r^{*}(x,y_{1})<r^{*}(x,y_{2})<\dots<r^{*}(x,y_{m}) (assuming that there is no tie in reward score). Let kk be the largest index for which r∗​(x,yk)≤αr^{*}(x,y_{k})\leq\alpha. Then

pA​(x)=∑i=1kPbase​(yi∣x)=F⁡(x,yk).p_{A}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{\text{base}}(y_{i}\mid x)=F(x,y_{k}). (226)

On the other hand, under the Best-of-NN sampling we have

PBoN​(Ax,α∣x)=∑i=1kPBoN​(yi∣x)=∑i=1k(F​(x,yi)N−F−​(x,yi)N)=F​(x,yk)N=pA​(x)N.P_{\text{BoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{\text{BoN}}(y_{i}\mid x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(F(x,y_{i})^{N}-F^{-}(x,y_{i})^{N})=F(x,y_{k})^{N}=p_{A}(x)^{N}. (227)

By assumption, ℋ\mathcal{H} contains f,g∈ℋf,g\in\mathcal{H} such that for any xx,

f⁡(x,y)−g⁡(x,y)={γ1if ​y∈Ax,αγ0otherwise.f(x,y)-g(x,y)=\begin{cases}\gamma_{1}&\text{if }y\in A_{x,\alpha}\\ \gamma_{0}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (228)

Denote ϕ=f−g\phi=f-g. For this choice,

λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)\displaystyle\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H}) ≤𝔼PBI​[(ϕ⁡(x,y)−ϕ⁡(x,y′))2]𝔼Q​[(ϕ⁡(x,y)−ϕ⁡(x,y′))2]\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{\text{BI}}}[(\phi(x,y)-\phi(x,y^{\prime}))^{2}]}{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\phi(x,y)-\phi(x,y^{\prime}))^{2}]} (229)
=PrPBI⁡(y∈Ax,α,y′∉Ax,α)+PrPBI⁡(y∉Ax,α,y′∈Ax,α)PrQ⁡(y∈Ax,α,y′∉Ax,α)+PrQ⁡(y∉Ax,α,y′∈Ax,α).\displaystyle=\frac{\Pr_{P_{\text{BI}}}(y\in A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\notin A_{x,\alpha})+\Pr_{P_{\text{BI}}}(y\notin A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\in A_{x,\alpha})}{\Pr_{Q}(y\in A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\notin A_{x,\alpha})+\Pr_{Q}(y\notin A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\in A_{x,\alpha})}. (230)

By assumption, the denominator is exactly γQ,α>0\gamma_{Q,\alpha}>0. For the numerator, first note that

ZI​(x)\displaystyle Z_{I}(x) =1−∑i=1m(FiN−Fi−1N)​pi\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N})p_{i} (231)
≥1−(maxi⁡pi)​∑i=1m(FiN−Fi−1N)\displaystyle\geq 1-(\max_{i}p_{i})\sum_{i=1}^{m}(F_{i}^{N}-F_{i-1}^{N}) (232)
≥1−maxi⁡pi\displaystyle\geq 1-\max_{i}p_{i} (233)
≥1−maxx,y⁡Pbase​(y∣x)=η.\displaystyle\geq 1-\max_{x,y}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)=\eta. (234)

Therefore,

PrPBI⁡(y∈Ax,α,y′∉Ax,α)+PrPBI⁡(y∉Ax,α,y′∈Ax,α)\displaystyle\Pr_{P_{\text{BI}}}(y\in A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\notin A_{x,\alpha})+\Pr_{P_{\text{BI}}}(y\notin A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\in A_{x,\alpha}) (235)
=𝔼x∼Px​[1ZI​(x)​(PBoN​(Ax,α∣x)​(1−pA​(x))+(1−PBoN​(Ax,α∣x))​pA​(x))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}\left[\frac{1}{Z_{I}(x)}\left(P_{\text{BoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)(1-p_{A}(x))+(1-P_{\text{BoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))p_{A}(x)\right)\right] (236)
≤1η​𝔼x∼Px​[pA​(x)N​(1−pA​(x))+(1−pA​(x)N)​pA​(x)]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}\left[p_{A}(x)^{N}(1-p_{A}(x))+(1-p_{A}(x)^{N})p_{A}(x)\right] (237)
≤1η​𝔼x∼Px​[pA​(x)N+pA​(x)].\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}\left[p_{A}(x)^{N}+p_{A}(x)\right]. (238)

Substituting back, we conclude that

λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)≤1η​γQ,α​𝔼x∼Px​[pA​(x)N+pA​(x)].\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\leq\frac{1}{\eta\gamma_{Q,\alpha}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}[p_{A}(x)^{N}+p_{A}(x)]. (239)

This proves the upper bound with DQ,α=1η​γQ,αD_{Q,\alpha}=\frac{1}{\eta\gamma_{Q,\alpha}}. ∎

B.2Connectivity bounds for PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}.

Let PbaseP_{\text{base}} be a base distribution. Then there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that for any NN,

λconn​(PBWI,Q,ℋ)≥C​(minx,y≠y′⁡Pbase​(y∣x)​Pbase​(y′∣x))N\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BWI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\geq C\Big(\min_{x,y\neq y^{\prime}}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\Big)^{N} (240)

On the other hand, for any real-valued α\alpha, we define the set of outcomes for which the reward is less than α\alpha for a given context xx as Ax,α={y∈𝒴:r∗​(x,y)≤α}A_{x,\alpha}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:r^{*}(x,y)\leq\alpha\}. For any α\alpha, if ℋ\mathcal{H} is flexible enough, then there exists a constant D>0D>0 such that for any NN,

λconn​(PBWI,Q,ℋ)≤D​𝔼x∼Px​[1+(Pbase​(Ax,α∣x))N​(1−Pbase​(Ax,α∣x))N]\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BWI}},Q;\mathcal{H})\leq D\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{x}}[1+(P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))^{N}(1-P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))^{N}] (241)
Proof.

Here we absorb the normalization constant of PBWIP_{\text{BWI}} into the constants. The proof is similar to the proof of Theorem B.1, except that we replace the calculation of the probability mass of PBIP_{\text{BI}} with that of PBWIP_{\text{BWI}}. We start with the lower bound,

PBWI​(x,y,y′)Q⁡(x,y,y′)\displaystyle\frac{P_{\text{BWI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})} =P⁡(x)​PBoN​(y∣x)​PWoN​(y′∣x)Q⁡(x,y,y′)\displaystyle=\frac{P(x)P_{\text{BoN}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{WoN}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})} (242)
=P⁡(x)​(F​(x,y)N−F−​(x,y)N)​((1−F−​(x,y′))N−(1−F⁡(x,y′))N)Q⁡(x,y,y′)\displaystyle=\frac{P(x)(F(x,y)^{N}-F^{-}(x,y)^{N})((1-F^{-}(x,y^{\prime}))^{N}-(1-F(x,y^{\prime}))^{N})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})} (243)
≥P⁡(x)​Pbase​(y∣x)N​Pbase​(y′∣x)NQ⁡(x,y,y′).\displaystyle\geq\frac{P(x)P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)^{N}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)^{N}}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}. (244)

Again, the term that decays with NN is Pbase​(y∣x)N​Pbase​(y′∣x)NP_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)^{N}P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)^{N}. So there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

PBWI​(x,y,y′)Q⁡(x,y,y′)≥C​(minx,y≠y′⁡Pbase​(y∣x)​Pbase​(y′∣x))N.\frac{P_{\text{BWI}}(x,y,y^{\prime})}{Q(x,y,y^{\prime})}\geq C\Big(\min_{x,y\neq y^{\prime}}P_{\text{base}}(y\mid x)P_{\text{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\Big)^{N}. (245)

For the upper bound, we first calculate the probability mass of PWoN​(Ax,α∣x)P_{\text{WoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x). We assume the same outcome ordering as in the proof of PBIP_{\text{BI}},

PWoN​(Ax,α∣x)\displaystyle P_{\text{WoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x) =∑i=1kPWoN​(yi∣x)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{\text{WoN}}(y_{i}\mid x) (246)
=∑i=1k((1−F−​(x,yi))N−(1−F⁡(x,yi))N)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}((1-F^{-}(x,y_{i}))^{N}-(1-F(x,y_{i}))^{N}) (247)
=1−(1−F⁡(x,yk))N\displaystyle=1-(1-F(x,y_{k}))^{N} (248)
=1−(1−Pbase​(Ax,α))N.\displaystyle=1-(1-P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}. (249)

With this, we have

PrPBWI⁡(y∈Ax,α,y′∉Ax,α)+PrPBWI⁡(y∉Ax,α,y′∈Ax,α)\displaystyle\Pr_{P_{\text{BWI}}}(y\in A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\notin A_{x,\alpha})+\Pr_{P_{\text{BWI}}}(y\notin A_{x,\alpha},y^{\prime}\in A_{x,\alpha}) (250)
=(PBoN​(Ax,α∣x))​(1−PWoN​(Ax,α∣x))+(1−PBoN​(Ax,α∣x))​(PWoN​(Ax,α∣x))\displaystyle=(P_{\text{BoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))(1-P_{\text{WoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))+(1-P_{\text{BoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x))(P_{\text{WoN}}(A_{x,\alpha}\mid x)) (251)
=(Pbase​(Ax,α))N​(1−Pbase​(Ax,α))N+(1−(Pbase​(Ax,α))N)​(1−(1−Pbase​(Ax,α))N)\displaystyle=(P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}(1-P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}+(1-(P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N})(1-(1-P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}) (252)
≤1+(Pbase​(Ax,α))N​(1−Pbase​(Ax,α))N.\displaystyle\leq 1+(P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}(1-P_{\text{base}}(A_{x,\alpha}))^{N}. (253)

∎

B.3General-QQ estimation error.

Let PP be a comparison distribution, let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a convex hypothesis class bounded by some constant BB, and let rP∗∈arg⁡minr∈ℋ​ℒP​(r)r^{*}_{P}\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{L}_{P}(r). Let SS be a set of nn i.i.d. samples drawn from PP, and let r^\hat{r} be the empirical risk minimizer of the BT learning objective based on SS. Then there exists a constant D>0D>0 such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

𝔼Q​[(Δr^−ΔrP∗)2]≤D​Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]\leq D\frac{\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta)}{\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})} (254)

where

Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ):=1σB​(ℜ^S​(ℋpair)+MB​log⁡(2/δ)n),\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta):=\frac{1}{\sigma_{B}}\left(\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{S}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{pair}})+M_{B}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{n}}\right), (255)

with MB:=log⁡(1+exp⁡(2​B))M_{B}:=\log(1+\exp(2B)) and σB:=σ⁡(2​B)​(1−σ⁡(2​B))\sigma_{B}:=\sigma(2B)(1-\sigma(2B)).

Proof.

If λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)=0\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})=0, the claim is vacuous. So assume that λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)>0\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})>0. By the definition of the connectivity degree,

𝔼Q​[(Δr^−ΔrP∗)2]≤1λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)​𝔼P​[(Δr^−ΔrP∗)2].\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})}\mathbb{E}_{P}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]. (256)

By Lemma A.7,

𝔼P​[(Δr^−ΔrP∗)2]=∥r^−rP∗∥Δ,P≤2σB​(ℒP​(r^)−ℒP​(rP∗)).\mathbb{E}_{P}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]=\lVert\hat{r}-r^{*}_{P}\rVert_{\Delta,P}\leq\frac{2}{\sigma_{B}}(\mathcal{L}_{P}(\hat{r})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})). (257)

Let ℒP^\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}} denote the empirical BT risk on the sample SS. Since r^\hat{r} is the empirical risk minimizer,

ℒP​(r^)−ℒP​(rP∗)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{P}(\hat{r})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P}) =(ℒP​(r^)−ℒP^​(r^))+(ℒP^​(r^)−ℒP^​(rP∗))+(ℒP^​(rP∗)−ℒP​(rP∗))\displaystyle=(\mathcal{L}_{P}(\hat{r})-\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(\hat{r}))+(\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(\hat{r})-\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(r^{*}_{P}))+(\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(r^{*}_{P})-\mathcal{L}_{P}(r^{*}_{P})) (258)
≤2​supr∈ℋ|ℒP​(r)−ℒP^​(r)|.\displaystyle\leq 2\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(r)|. (259)

Now let ℓ⁡(a)=−log⁡σ⁡(a)\ell(a)=-\log\sigma(a). Since ℋ\mathcal{H} is bounded by BB, we have |r⁡(x,y)−r⁡(x,y′)|≤2​B|r(x,y)-r(x,y^{\prime})|\leq 2B, so

ℓ⁡(a)≤log⁡(1+exp⁡(2​B)):=MB\ell(a)\leq\log(1+\exp(2B)):=M_{B} (260)

for all relevant aa. Moreover, ℓ\ell is 11-Lipschitz. Therefore, by the standard Rademacher-complexity bound and the contraction lemma, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

supr∈ℋ|ℒP​(r)−ℒP^​(r)|≤2​ℜ^S​(ℋpair)+3​MB​log⁡(2/δ)n.\sup_{r\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathcal{L}_{P}(r)-\widehat{\mathcal{L}_{P}}(r)|\leq 2\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{S}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{pair}})+3M_{B}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{n}}. (261)

Combining the last three displays, we obtain

𝔼Q​[(Δr^−ΔrP∗)2]≤1λconn​(P,Q,ℋ)​(8σB​ℜ^S​(ℋpair)+12​MBσB​log⁡(2/δ)n).\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{P}})^{2}]\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P,Q;\mathcal{H})}\left(\frac{8}{\sigma_{B}}\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{S}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{pair}})+\frac{12M_{B}}{\sigma_{B}}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{n}}\right). (262)

Absorbing the numerical factors into a constant DD proves the lemma. ∎

See 5.7

Proof.

Since rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}} preserves the ranking induced by r∗r^{*}, the sign-based accuracy with respect to r∗r^{*} is the same as the sign-based accuracy with respect to rBI∗r^{*}_{\text{BI}}. By Lemma B.3 applied with P=PBIP=P_{\text{BI}} and rP∗=rBI∗r^{*}_{P}=r^{*}_{\text{BI}}, there exists a constant D>0D>0 such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

𝔼Q​[(Δr^−ΔrBI∗)2]≤D​Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ).\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}})^{2}]\leq D\frac{\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta)}{\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})}. (263)

For any threshold u>0u>0, order preservation implies

AccQ⁡(r^)\displaystyle\operatorname{Acc}_{Q}(\hat{r}) ≥PrQ⁡(|Δr^−ΔrBI∗|≤|ΔrBI∗|)\displaystyle\geq\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|\leq|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|) (264)
≥PrQ⁡(|ΔrBI∗|≥u)−PrQ⁡(|Δr^−ΔrBI∗|>u)\displaystyle\geq\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|\geq u)-\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|>u) (265)
≥PrQ⁡(|ΔrBI∗|≥u)−𝔼Q​[(Δr^−ΔrBI∗)2]u2\displaystyle\geq\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|\geq u)-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[(\Delta_{\hat{r}}-\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}})^{2}]}{u^{2}} (266)
≥PrQ⁡(|ΔrBI∗|≥u)−D​Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)u2​λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ),\displaystyle\geq\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|\geq u)-D\frac{\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta)}{u^{2}\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})}, (267)

where the third line follows from Markov’s inequality.

Next, we use Proposition 5.2. Because 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} are finite and every triplet in the support of QQ has non-zero probability mass under Pbase(⋅∣x)P_{\text{base}}(\cdot\mid x), the uniform boundedness of BN​(x,y,y′)B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}) implies that

MQ:=max⁡supN≥1(x,y,y′)∈supp⁡(Q)⁡|BN​(x,y,y′)|<∞.M_{Q}:=\max_{(x,y,y^{\prime})\in\operatorname{supp}(Q)}\sup_{N\geq 1}|B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime})|<\infty. (268)

For every (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}) in the support of QQ, Proposition 5.2 gives

ΔrBI∗​(x,y,y′)=N​log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)+BN​(x,y,y′).\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(x;y,y^{\prime})=N\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}+B_{N}(x;y,y^{\prime}). (269)

Therefore,

|ΔrBI∗​(x,y,y′)|≥N​|log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)|−MQ.|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(x;y,y^{\prime})|\geq N\left|\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}\right|-M_{Q}. (270)

In particular, for any k>0k>0,

|log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)|≥k+MQN⟹|ΔrBI∗​(x,y,y′)|≥N​k.\left|\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}\right|\geq k+\frac{M_{Q}}{N}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}(x;y,y^{\prime})|\geq Nk. (271)

Hence,

PrQ⁡(|ΔrBI∗|≥N​k)≥PrQ⁡(|log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)|≥k+MQN).\Pr_{Q}(|\Delta_{r^{*}_{\text{BI}}}|\geq Nk)\geq\Pr_{Q}\left(\left|\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}\right|\geq k+\frac{M_{Q}}{N}\right). (272)

Substituting u=N​ku=Nk into the accuracy bound above yields

AccQ⁡(r^)≥supk>0[PrQ⁡(|log⁡F⁡(x,y)F⁡(x,y′)|≥k+MQN)−D​Comp⁡(n,ℋ,δ)N2​k2​λconn​(PBI,Q,ℋ)].\displaystyle\operatorname{Acc}_{Q}(\hat{r})\geq\sup_{k>0}\Big[\Pr_{Q}\left(\left|\log\frac{F(x,y)}{F(x,y^{\prime})}\right|\geq k+\frac{M_{Q}}{N}\right)-D\frac{\operatorname{Comp}(n,\mathcal{H},\delta)}{N^{2}k^{2}\lambda_{\text{conn}}(P_{\text{BI}},Q;\mathcal{H})}\Big]. (273)

This is the desired result. ∎

Appendix C Experiment details

In this section, we provide full experimental details and additional results that supplement the main experiments. We conduct experiments on synthetic data to validate our theoretical findings, following the setup of Pukdee et al. (2026).

C.1 Synthetic Data Setup

Context and Response Space. Let 𝒮={u1,u2,…,um}\mathcal{S}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{m}\} be a finite set of items with ui∈ℝdu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let 𝒳=𝒴=𝒮\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{S}. We use the same space for contexts and responses to simplify the synthetic setting, so the score function can be interpreted as a similarity function between items. We set m=16m=16 and d=128d=128 for simplicity. To generate the dataset, we sample each uiu_{i} from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

Ground-truth Score Function. The ground-truth score is defined via a two-layer neural network f∗:ℝd→ℝef^{*}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{e} with hidden dimension h=32h=32 and output embedding dimension e=8e=8, using ReLU activations:

r∗​(x,y)=cosine−similarity⁡(f∗​(x),f∗​(y)),r^{*}(x,y)=\operatorname{cosine-similarity}(f^{*}(x),f^{*}(y)), (274)

ensuring scores lie in [−1,1][-1,1].

Triplet Generation. We generate nn triplets S={(xi,yi+,yi−)}i=1nS=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{+},y_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{n} by sampling xix_{i} uniformly from 𝒳\mathcal{X} and drawing yi+y_{i}^{+} and yi−y_{i}^{-} from a negative distribution p−(⋅∣xi)p^{-}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) and a positive distribution p+(⋅∣xi)p^{+}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) that is BT-consistent with r∗r^{*}, i.e., log⁡(p+​(y∣x)/p−​(y∣x))=r∗​(x,y)\log(p^{+}(y\mid x)/p^{-}(y\mid x))=r^{*}(x,y). By default, we use a uniform negative distribution p−(⋅∣x)=1mp^{-}(\cdot\mid x)=\frac{1}{m}. The validation set is also generated in the same way.

Training and Evaluation. We train a two-layer neural network with the same architecture as f∗f^{*} to minimize the empirical BT loss on SS. We use the Adam optimizer with learning rate selected from {10−4,10−3,10−2}\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\}. We train for 200 epochs and select hyperparameters via a validation set of 2048 triplets drawn from the same distribution based on validation loss. We report accuracy with respect to the uniform distribution QQ over all pairs (ui,uj)(u_{i},u_{j}), with standard error over 5 random seeds.

C.6 Details on distribution reshaping

To modify the shape of the base distribution in a standardized way, we use upsampling and downsampling. Each time we sample a response from the base distribution, we accept it with probability 1−p1-p. Otherwise, we evaluate its reward score. If the score lies in the percentile range [c−w/2,c+w/2][c-w/2,c+w/2] for the given context xx, then we accept the response in the upsampling setting and reject it in the downsampling setting; outside this range, we do the opposite. We repeat this process until we obtain N=4N=4 responses, and then apply the Best-vs-Random mechanism to generate the training data. Equivalently, this procedure increases or decreases the probability mass in a specified score band, yielding the modified base distributions

Pbase,up∝(1−p)​Pbase+p​Pc,wP_{\text{base,up}}\propto(1-p)P_{\text{base}}+pP_{c,w} (275)
Pbase,down∝(1−p)​Pbase−p​Pc,wP_{\text{base,down}}\propto(1-p)P_{\text{base}}-pP_{c,w} (276)

where Pc,wP_{c,w} denotes the base distribution with probability mass concentrated in the region whose reward score lies in the percentile range [c−w/2,c+w/2][c-w/2,c+w/2]. Here cc is the percentile center and ww is the width of the band. We use c∈{15,30,50,70,85}c\in\{15,30,50,70,85\}, w=30w=30, and p=0.8p=0.8. This up/downsampling procedure provides a standardized way to reshape the base distribution. For example, setting c=15c=15 targets lower-score responses, while setting c=85c=85 targets higher-score responses. We use n=512n=512 samples for each dataset and train a reward model with the same setup as in the previous experiments.

C.7 Distribution of the reward score under different base distributions

C.8 Additional details for GSM8K

GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021a) is a question-answering dataset rather than a preference dataset, so we construct preference pairs from model-generated responses. For each prompt in the test set, we sample multiple responses from the base generator and score them with the reward model. Each response is labeled as correct or incorrect by extracting the final numeric answer and comparing it to the gold answer. We then pair a randomly selected correct response against the highest-scoring incorrect response (i.e., the most convincing wrong answer according to the reward model), and discard prompts that lack either a correct or incorrect response.

A complication is that the reward model is poorly calibrated for mathematical correctness on GSM8K: the score distributions for correct and incorrect responses overlap substantially, meaning a non-trivial fraction of correct responses receive lower reward scores than incorrect ones from the same prompt. To avoid contaminating the test set with pairs where the reward model effectively disagrees with the ground-truth labeling, we additionally require the chosen (correct) response to outscore the rejected (incorrect) response by a reward margin of at least 2. Figure 17(a) shows the resulting score distributions: even after this filter, the chosen and rejected distributions remain heavily overlapping, indicating that the test set is far from trivial.
